Path Who holds your ticket and SSH connection What comes back to the model The agent's own shell (ssh cluster cat …) nobody: it fails, because the sandbox (Mode A: Claude Code's; Mode B: phiward's) hides your keys, config and connection socket. With phiward's hook alone and no sandbox it would not fail. nothing The gateway (phiward copy, phiward run --remote) your broker, outside the sandbox masked output

How a remote run goes:

sequenceDiagram
  participant A as The agent (sandboxed)
  participant B as Your broker (your computer)
  participant S as Your shared SSH connection
  participant C as The cluster
  A->>B: phiward run --remote hpc -- squeue -u you
  B->>S: the listed program, through your connection
  S->>C: runs as you
  Note over C: Nothing confines the command on the cluster: keep to counts
  C-->>B: output
  B-->>A: output, with protected paths masked (not bare names)

docs.title: One-time setup
docs.text:
The easy way: phiward setup, answer yes to the HPC question, and give the cluster's short name, login host, your user name and your work folder. It writes phiward's ssh config and the [copy] and [remote] settings, and prints the lines for your ~/.ssh/config. Then do step 4 below. The steps by hand, which do the same:

Use one host name everywhere below (here hpc).

  1. In ~/.ssh/config, add these lines to your existing entry for host hpc (keep its HostName, User and GSSAPIAuthentication lines):
  ControlMaster auto
  ControlPath ~/.ssh/cm-%C
  ControlPersist 8h
  1. Write phiward's own ssh config, ~/.config/phiward/ssh_config, with the same Host, HostName, User and ControlPath, and ControlMaster no:
Host hpc
  HostName <login host>
  User <you>
  ControlPath ~/.ssh/cm-%C
  ControlMaster no

%C stands for the host, user and port, so they must be the same in both files. 3. Edit ~/.config/phiward/config.toml. - In the [copy] section, add ssh_config = "~/.config/phiward/ssh_config", and make sure remotes holds your HPC work folder. setup may have made this section already: do not add a second [copy] section; a second one makes the file invalid. - Add a [remote] section at the end:

[remote]
hosts = ["hpc"]
commands = ["squeue", "sacct", "sinfo"]
roots = ["/data/protected"]

Then run phiward doctor: a mistake in the file shows as a PROBLEM. If the broker runs already, restart it: it refuses requests after the config changes, until you do (setup.md). 4. Before each session that uses HPC, in Terminal:

kinit you@REALM

ssh -fN hpc
  1. Test it:
phiward run --remote hpc -- squeue -u you

The sections below explain what each part does and allows.

docs.title: What the session can never use
docs.text:
• your Kerberos ticket caches that are files: the file KRB5CCNAME names, krb5cc* files in /tmp, /var/tmp and the macOS per-user temp folder, and /run/user/<uid> on Linux. A cache kept by the macOS credential service (API:, the default when KRB5CCNAME is not set) or by the Linux keyring or KCM is not a file; Mode B blocks the Linux keyring, and doctor warns when your cache is not a file (modes.md);
  • ~/.ssh (keys, config, known hosts), the SSH agent, and the socket of your shared connection (outside unix sockets are refused).

docs.title: Mounted HPC storage
docs.text: Put the mount path of protected HPC folders in your protected roots (for example the folder where the cluster's protected storage is mounted on your Mac), with phiward setup or in the user config. On Linux, phiward also protects other mounts of the same data that it can see (alias mounts). On macOS it does not detect them: list every mount path of the data as a root. phiward run -- CMD on that data runs through the broker, with masked output.

docs.title: Your shared connection holds the login
docs.text:
Every request to HPC (a copy to or from a remote, run --remote) goes through your shared SSH connection. You start it; phiward's ssh joins it through its control socket, which needs no key and no ticket. So: - no request can read ~/.ssh (keys, config, known hosts), a ticket cache or a keytab; - a request has no network except that one socket, and only the system ssh, with options phiward fixes (no forwarding of any kind), ever talks to it; - if the connection is not running, the request is refused with a message. phiward never logs in by itself.

The socket carries your full login: a program that could speak ssh's protocol on it could ask your connection for forwarding or new channels. That is why nothing but the system ssh touches it (rsync does not), and why phiward trusts a socket only when it is yours, is not a link, and lies under ~/.ssh (or /run/user/<uid>) in folders that only you can write: a socket the agent made first somewhere else is refused. On Linux a request also gets fresh, empty /tmp, /var/tmp and home folders, so the sockets there are out of reach; a socket in another folder you can write (for example /scratch) that was renamed after it was made is not, but only ssh runs there. Files your ssh config Includes from your home are not visible to it on Linux.

Keep phiward's ssh config outside ~/.ssh. Its ControlPath must be under ~/.ssh (setup step 2).

[remote] use_shared_connection = false turns this off: ssh then logs in itself, so a request can read your key or ticket and has the network. The agent still cannot choose ssh's options or the paths, but a bug in ssh or rsync that the other end exploits could then reach a credential.

docs.title: phiward copy
docs.text:
phiward copy SRC... DST copies without printing names. The destination must be inside one of your protected roots (by its real path, with no link on the way, and not a pattern match or a .claude folder), or under a remote you approved in the user config. A .claude folder is never copied:

[copy]
remotes = ["hpc:/work/yourname/project"]
ssh_config = "~/.config/phiward/ssh_config"
push_limit_gib = 5        # a larger push is yours to do (default 5)

A remote must name a work folder on the cluster: not /, not a folder just below it (/home, /data), not a home folder (a folder named home, home1, homes or users, or one just inside it, wherever it is: /home/you, /gpfs/home/you), and not inside a dot-folder (.ssh, .config). setup refuses these, and copy ignores such a remote. A copy never goes into a dot-folder either. A push to your home folder could otherwise plant your login files there; if your cluster names home folders another way, name a work folder yourself.

Copies may go: - from an unprotected folder (the project) to an approved remote, under a [remote] roots folder; - from a protected folder to a protected folder or to an approved remote, under a [remote] roots folder; - from an approved remote to a protected folder.

Give local paths in full: a local path with a .. part, or one that starts with a quoted ~, is refused. A push goes only under a [remote] roots folder, where remote output is masked; with no remote root, every push is refused (setup makes each new copy remote's folder one). Locally, what lands is inside a protected root. On the cluster it is masked only under [remote] roots, and a link there can carry a push outside one.

A push (local sources to a remote) does not use rsync. A source may be any file or folder that is not a credential, not above one, and not in /dev, /proc or /sys. Your broker checks each source, resolves it once, opens it without following links, and sends what it reads as a tar stream to tar -x in the remote folder (made if missing). So: - a link put on a source path after the check makes the push stop; nothing behind it is sent; - links, special files and files with a second name (hard links) inside a source are skipped and counted, never followed; - files that a shell, ssh or a tool reads at login or when you enter a folder are skipped and counted, at any depth: .ssh, .bashrc, .profile, .zshrc, .gitconfig, .envrc, .config, .local, .ipython, .Rprofile and similar; and every name that starts with . at the top of the destination. Copy them yourself if you need them there; - the remote side cannot ask for anything: the stream goes one way; - src lands as DEST/src, src/ and src/. land as its contents; the destination is a folder; - every push sends everything named (no resume), but files that exist on the cluster are kept, never replaced, and pushed files arrive without the executable bit (0644; folders 0755): an agent cannot replace a job script you run later. To update a file there, delete it yourself first, or chmod +x a script you pushed; - over push_limit_gib, the push is refused: copy it yourself.

The result is counts (copy sent: files=N folders=N skipped=N) and whatever the remote side prints, masked like run --remote output (your [remote] roots included).

A pull (remote sources to a protected folder) does not use rsync either: tar -c on the remote streams through the shared connection into a local tar -x that runs in the gateway profile. It writes only inside protected roots, reads no credential and has no network at all. Every pull sends everything named (no resume); files that exist in the protected folder are kept, never replaced. What the remote sends lands inside the protected folder: plain files and folders only; links and special files are skipped.

A remote path may hold only letters, digits and . _ + - /, so it is one plain word for the remote shell. An argument with a : before its first / is remote, as rsync reads it: write a local name with a : as ./name. A source that is or holds a credential (~/.ssh, your home) is refused. A copy between two remotes is refused.

docs.title: phiward run --remote HOST -- CMD
docs.text:
Your broker runs CMD on the host through your shared connection, and masks what comes back.

[remote]
hosts = ["cluster"]                     # hosts the agent may name
commands = ["squeue", "sacct", "sinfo", "wc", "du"]   # programs it may run there; empty = none
roots = ["/data/protected"]                # protected paths on the host, masked in the output

phiward run --remote cluster -- squeue -u yourname
  • Only hosts in [remote] hosts and programs in [remote] commands are allowed. These keys come from your user config only; a repo config cannot set them. The program is one bare name. Every word reaches the remote shell quoted, so ;, $() and the like are plain text there. A word with !, a newline or another control character is refused: a csh or tcsh login shell expands ! even inside quotes.
  • Nothing confines the command on the cluster. It runs as you. The list of commands is what limits its effects there. Each program you add is a decision: sbatch submits a job that can run anything, and cat or head print contents, which masking does not hide beyond names and identifiers.
  • The output is masked like local gateway output: your protected roots, the names under them, identifier patterns, names files and packs, plus every path under [remote] roots, in its absolute spellings (//, /./). A word with a .. part is refused. After a remote root, the rest of the path up to a tab or the end of the line is masked, since a name may hold spaces: put counts before paths (wc, du do). Not covered: a path relative to the remote folder (../share/P1), a remote link to a protected folder, and bare names (below).
  • Bare names are not masked. phiward cannot list what is under a remote root, so a name printed without its path (ls /data/protected, find -printf %f) passes unless a pack, a pattern or a names file catches it. Do not list commands such as ls or find in [remote] commands for protected folders.
  • It uses the system ssh with -F your [copy] ssh_config, through the shared connection's socket, with BatchMode=yes, no proxy or local command, no forwarding, no terminal.
  • Tested against a real cluster from macOS: remote runs, a push, a pull into a protected folder, a refused push of ~/.ssh, the session's own ssh failing, and a refusal with the shared connection stopped.

docs.title: Claude Code on the login node
docs.text:
You can also run Claude Code on the HPC login node itself, as one user without admin rights. Its sandbox then confines the shell there (Mode A), with phiward's hook. The gateway works there only on a kernel with Landlock (see below). Check first that your site allows interactive tools on its login nodes.

What the node needs:

  • Landlock ABI 2 or newer in the kernel (Linux 5.19 or newer) for the gateway: phiward run refuses to run without it. A RHEL 8 node (kernel 4.18) has no Landlock: there the hook and Claude Code's sandbox work, and the gateway does not. phiward doctor says which.
  • bubblewrap 0.4 or newer with user namespaces (RHEL 8 has 0.4.0). phiward doctor checks the version.
  • socat on the PATH. Without admin rights, make a conda environment for it in your own space, for example mamba create -p /scratch/$USER/claude-env -c conda-forge socat, and put its bin folder first on the PATH before you start Claude Code. (sandbox.socatPath would name it too, but Claude Code reads it only from managed settings.)
  • Claude Code 2.1.295 or newer, as everywhere. It tells the hook which MCP server each tool belongs to. bash tools/check-claude-mcp-source.sh (from a phiward checkout) shows what yours sends.

Then, in your own terminal on the node:

  1. (cd ~ && phiward setup): protect the data folders as roots. On Linux, protected patterns make the hook refuse shell commands, so use roots.
  2. (cd ~ && phiward install claude --user --write). It writes the hooks and sandbox entries into ~/.claude/settings.json, and the file for claude --settings.
  3. Start Claude Code with that file, for example with an alias in your own shell startup file: alias claude='claude --settings ~/.config/phiward/claude-settings.json'. With it, the sandbox is admin-required without admin rights: a repository's settings cannot turn it off, exclude commands or add writable folders.
  4. Start the broker in a terminal of its own on the node, and run phiward doctor.

A probe of Claude Code's sandbox engine (@anthropic-ai/sandbox-runtime 0.0.81) on a RHEL 8 login node (kernel 4.18, bubblewrap 0.4.0) passed all 21 tests:

  • a made-up root under /scratch was hidden by its real path, through a home folder link (~/work -> ...) and by a wildcard;
  • the project and the temporary folder stayed writable;
  • the settings files, .mcp.json, .bashrc and the folders next to the project could not be written;
  • the direct network was blocked.

A home folder on NFS was not part of that probe. The release check with the real Claude Code (scripts/sandbox-check/check.sh, releasing.md) runs on Linux too; it has not been run on the cluster yet.

docs.title: Rules for the operator
docs.text:
• Start the shared connection yourself; phiward never logs in.
  • Until you trust the lists you wrote, read every HPC request the agent proposes before it runs (Claude Code asks you before it runs a command, unless you allowed it). This is your habit, not a phiward feature: phiward itself never asks at run time; your config decides.
  • Keep [remote] commands short. Prefer commands that print counts and states.
  • The HPC side's own rules (partitions, job names, where clinical data may be read) still apply.
  • The release check's remote probes (REMOTE, REMOTE_DIR) use an ssh config of their own that can only join the shared connection you start for them (no key, no ticket). Give a new, empty folder: the check writes only under it, and deletes nothing. Remove it yourself afterwards.

Next: daily use.

docs.title: Mode B: the agent tool under phiward launch
docs.text:
• For: people who run the agent in a terminal and want the whole tool confined.
  • Before: the quick start, steps 1 and 2.
  • You will have: sessions in phiward's kernel profile, with settings you approve.

phiward launch --tool claude runs the whole agent tool, and everything it starts, inside the kernel profile: its file tools, shell, MCP servers and hooks. The tool cannot read your protected data, whatever the model asks it to do. You work with protected data through the gateway (phiward run, phiward copy), which masks what comes back. This is the strongest mode (Mode B). A normal Claude Code session wired by the hook (Mode A) is the other; modes.md compares them.

Tested with the real Claude Code on macOS: reads of protected data by the file tools and the shell were refused, and the gateway returned masked output. Mode B is for the terminal: driving a launch session from the desktop app with Remote Control is not tested yet.

How a session's settings stay trusted:

flowchart TD
  A["The trusted copy (what you added with carryover add)"] --> B["A fresh folder for this session"]
  B --> C["The session runs in the kernel profile"]
  C --> D["What it changed goes to quarantine"]
  D --> E{"phiward carryover show: you read it"}
  E -->|"accept"| A
  E -->|"leave it"| F["Not used by later sessions"]

docs.title: Once
docs.text:
1. Install and set up: steps 1 and 2 of the quick start.
  2. A login token, because each session starts in a fresh config folder: run claude setup-token in a plain terminal, open the URL, approve, and keep the token it prints. Then, in the terminal where you start sessions:
export CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN='<the token>'

The agent can read this variable, like an API key. Revoke it in your Claude account settings when you no longer need it. 3. The broker must run (for run and copy): best as a login service (setup.md), or phiward broker in a terminal of its own.

docs.title: Every session
docs.text:
From the project folder:

phiward launch --tool claude
  • --memory: turn Claude Code's auto memory on. It then lives in the session's folder, and its changes go to quarantine like any other instruction.
  • launch refuses to start in /, your home, a folder above or inside protected data, a dot folder, ~/Library, a folder on your PATH, or a phiward folder.
  • Several launch sessions may run side by side, also in one project (see limit L8 of the threat model).

docs.title: What a session can and cannot do
docs.text: Can Cannot Files read and write the project; write its own session folder and the spool read protected roots, patterns or derived folders (.git, snapshots, and on Linux other mounts of the same data); read credentials (~/.ssh, ~/.aws, ~/.claude, other agent tools' logins, browser profiles, Kerberos tickets and keytabs, SSH keys your SSH config names, research-data and registry logins), shell histories, the Trash, or the gateway's write_to folders; write anywhere else Settings that run later change .mcp.json, .claude/settings*.json, .vscode settings, or git control files (hooks, config) in the project. On Linux a git control file that is missing at the start (commondir) can be made; the report at the end names it. A wrapped MCP server (--entry) cannot write the project's .git folders, .claude or .vscode; on macOS also .idea, .gitmodules, .ripgreprc or a new .git (on Linux a name missing at the start can be made) Processes run any program in the profile read other terminals, signal processes outside, inject keystrokes, open or script other apps Network open in this release (see Limits) reach outside unix sockets (the SSH agent, your shared SSH connection, docker) Protected data phiward run -- CMD (masked output), phiward copy (no names printed) anything else

docs.title: When a session ends
docs.text:
• The session's folder is thrown away. Each session starts from a trusted copy in ~/.phiward/carryover/claude/, which no session can read or write. Nothing is shared between sessions: no transcripts, no login, no caches.
  • Instruction changes go to quarantine. These are files Claude Code reads as instructions or settings (CLAUDE.md, rules/, skills/, agents/, commands/, plugins you install, settings.json), and the MCP and permission keys of .claude.json. The exit message lists them:
phiward carryover show --tool claude
phiward carryover accept ID [ITEM...] --tool claude
phiward carryover add PATH [--as NAME] --tool claude   # your own CLAUDE.md, a skill
phiward carryover status --tool claude                 # sizes; what is safe to delete

accept ID settings.json takes the whole settings.json as the session left it; show lists the keys that changed, and for .claude.json the value accept writes, so read it first. Items you do not name stay in quarantine. add ~/.claude.json takes only its MCP servers, trust and allowed-tools keys, never the login or the history; an MCP server's env and header values there are readable by the agent. - The project report. It lists every file the session changed that is read as instructions for models (CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, .claude/), every file that runs later (git control files of any repository, hooks, build files, .pth, scripts, executables) and every settings file. Other changed files are named when there are 10 or fewer, and otherwise only counted; code under .venv or node_modules is in that count. In a very large project it says so, and past its limit checks only the first three kinds (dot folders such as .claude first); past 2,000,000 entries it checks nothing more. Treat everything in the project as written by the agent, and read it before you run anything outside launch. - Anything under ~/.phiward may be deleted at any time (a disk quota, an HPC purge, or you). The next start rebuilds from what is left, and it never trusts a folder a session could write. carryover status says what each deletion costs.

docs.title: HPC
docs.text: See hpc.md: HPC through your Kerberos ticket and mounts, copy to approved remotes, and run --remote for commands on HPC.

docs.title: Linux: the session's view
docs.text:
On Linux the session sees a snapshot of the file system. Every folder above a protected path or a credential (for example /, /home, your home) is rebuilt for the session from the entries it held at the start, without the protected ones. A protected folder replaced at its path, and a pattern match, credential or ticket cache made after the start, are not in the view.

What this costs: - An entry the host adds to one of those folders after the start (a new folder in your home) is seen only by the next session. A file the host replaces there (an editor saving ~/.gitconfig) stays as it was for the session. - A folder that is missing from the view cannot be made: mkdir ~/.ssh fails (read-only). - A folder that can be entered but not listed (mode 711, common on HPC) cannot be rebuilt. It is shown whole, with the protected roots and credentials in it masked; one made in it later is not hidden. - On Linux the view must fit in bwrap's 9000 arguments, about three for each entry it rebuilds. A protected folder below a folder of thousands of entries (a large data folder) would need more, so launch shows such folders whole instead, those that save the most first, and says before the tool starts how many folders it shows whole. In those folders, as in a 711 folder, a protected entry made or replaced after the start is not hidden. A folder shown whole lists its masked entries by name, so the folder that holds a protected root, or where a pattern's * names the protected entries, is never shown whole: if the view cannot fit then, launch refuses, and you protect that folder as a root instead (/data/study rather than /data/study/<name>). launch also counts bwrap's whole command line before it starts and says so when it is too long. A pattern whose * falls on a folder that cannot be listed cannot cover it: launch refuses, and you protect that folder as a root instead. - A pattern follows a linked folder only in its literal part (/data/... through /data -> /gpfs/...), not at a * level: a match reached through a link there is hidden at the link only. Protect the target as a root.

Protection follows the path, on Linux and macOS. A protected folder that you move into a folder the session can see is readable there, during a session or after it.

docs.title: Self-check
docs.text:
It also reports start-up files next to phiward (.pth, sitecustomize in any form) that no install record lists, or that changed since install. One it cannot check: _virtualenv.py, which uv's and virtualenv's environments add and no record lists.

launch checks its own installed files against the installer's record first, in a separate Python that reads no compiled files. A changed file, a compiled file that does not match its source, or a file the record does not list makes it refuse: reinstall. Without a record (a source checkout or an editable install) it refuses unless PHIWARD_DEV=1 is set. It cannot find code that changes the launcher itself so that the check is skipped, and it trusts the installer's record: a process running as you that changes a file and its record line is not found. It is meant to catch what a session without launch left behind by mistake or by a careless agent; when in doubt, reinstall: the step names the command for the tool that installed phiward.

docs.title: Limits in this release
docs.text:
• Not hidden: shell start-up files (~/.zshrc, which may export tokens), ~/.gitconfig (which may hold an http.extraheader), and, on macOS, Keychain items whose access list trusts the security tool (the session can reach the Keychain service). Keep tokens out of start-up files; prefer Mode A's test result for Keychain-backed tokens until Mode B is checked.
  • Git control files are read-only for the repositories found at the start, so git remote add, git config, git submodule update --init, git worktree add and git push -u fail inside launch (and git switch to a remote branch, git branch -u, -m and -d cannot record their settings: git switch still prints "set up to track" but does not); run them in your own terminal. A repository the session makes is not read-only, but its control files are listed in the exit report as files that run later.
  • Linux: Claude Code's own sandbox runs inside launch. phiward turns it off only on macOS. On Linux its bubblewrap starts inside phiward's, and where the host refuses a user namespace inside bubblewrap, Claude Code's Bash tool fails (visibly: the command is refused, nothing runs unconfined).
  • A launch inside a session (a wrapped MCP server, or a launch for another project) runs its command directly, under the session's own profile: not the narrower profile of a server (which keeps more of the project read-only), and not another project's .phiward.toml. On macOS a file only that profile denies tells launch it is inside; on Linux the session's seccomp filter answers one unused system call with an error number nothing else gives. Anything else (no filter, another sandbox's filter) builds the full profile; where ~/.phiward cannot be written, that launch refuses and nothing runs.

Read threat-model.md (Mode B, limits L1–L8). In short: - The network is open. A session cannot read protected data, so it cannot send it. But it can carry out what it can read: gateway output (masked), the login token, the project. - macOS: a process that leaves the tool's process tree keeps running after the session (L5). It can no longer change what a later session reads, but it can write the project. Close the terminal after a session. - macOS: the Keychain and the per-user temp folder are shared with your own tools. - Masking covers names and identifiers, not content. Through the gateway, print counts and summaries, not records (rule 3 of the agent rules that phiward init adds to AGENTS.md). Dates can be masked with the dates pack. - tmux, script and other tools that open a new terminal do not work yet. - Other tools than Claude Code run under launch -- PROGRAM with the boundary, but without a per-session config folder (no adapter yet).

Next: what Mode B does not cover is in the threat model.

docs.title: Choose a mode: a Claude Code session (Mode A) or phiward launch (Mode B)
docs.text:
For: anyone who chooses between the two modes, or decides whether phiward is enough.

phiward protects protected data in two ways. Both use the same user config, the same broker and the same gateway (phiward run, phiward copy, phiward run --remote), so work on protected data is equally protected in both. What differs is how much of the agent tool itself is confined. Words are explained in the glossary.

What confines what, in Mode A:

flowchart TD
  A["Claude Code session (app, IDE or terminal)"] --> B["Bash commands"]
  A --> C["File tools: Read, Grep, Edit"]
  A --> D["MCP servers and hooks"]
  B --> E["Claude Code's sandbox (kernel)"]
  C --> F["phiward's hook and permission rules"]
  D --> G["your rights (an MCP server: unless it is wrapped)"]

And in Mode B:

flowchart TD
  A["phiward launch"] --> B["the whole agent tool: shell, file tools, MCP servers, hooks"]
  B --> C["phiward's kernel profile"]

In both, work on protected data goes through the gateway.

The hidden list (both modes): credentials (~/.ssh, ~/.aws, ~/.config/gh, other agent tools' and the Claude app's logins, browser profiles), Kerberos ticket caches and keytabs, SSH keys your ssh configs name, shell and REPL histories, the Trash, thumbnails, local IPC sockets. In Mode A, install puts it in Claude Code's sandbox and permission rules, and the hook refuses it; in Mode B the kernel hides it. Gateway commands cannot read it either. In Mode A, Claude Code's own folder (~/.claude: memory, plans, skills, saved tool output) stays usable; only its login files (.credentials.json, ~/.claude.json) are hidden.

Mode A: a Claude Code session Mode B: phiward launch Start open the project as usual: the desktop app, an IDE, or claude in a terminal phiward launch --tool claude in a terminal (terminal only for now: driving it from the app with Remote Control is not tested) Set up phiward setup (it wires your user settings), once; phiward init in each project with protected work launch.md, once Bash commands in Claude Code's own sandbox (the kernel): protected paths and the hidden list cannot be read in phiward's kernel profile File tools (Read, Grep, Glob, Edit) refused by phiward's hook and by Claude Code's permission rules (inside Claude Code, not the kernel) in phiward's kernel profile MCP servers your full rights, unless you wrap each one (below) confined Hooks your full rights confined Your ~/.claude (skills, rules, MCP config) used as it is each session starts from a trusted copy (carryover add); changes go to quarantine Work on protected data the gateway the gateway Use it for day-to-day work, every protected step through the gateway long sessions close to protected data, or untrusted input (web pages, other people's repositories)

docs.title: What Mode A does not do
docs.text:
• It does not cover a session that skips the settings. claude --bare (often used for scripts and CI) skips every hook, plugin, MCP server and CLAUDE.md, and an Agent SDK app with settingSources: [] loads no settings file. Then neither phiward's hook nor its sandbox and deny rules apply, and nothing says so. In scripts, run claude -p without --bare; in an SDK app, load the user settings (settingSources: ["user", "project", "local"]), pass phiward install claude --json as its settings, or run the whole program under phiward launch. See unattended.md.
  • The file tools are refused inside Claude Code, not by the kernel. A path spelling that both the permission rules and the hook miss reads the file. The hook resolves links and spellings, and Claude Code's deny rules also match a link's target, so this needs a gap in both.
  • Hooks and MCP servers that are not wrapped run with your rights: one could read protected data.
  • On Linux, protected patterns cannot be confined by Claude Code's sandbox (roots only): with patterns, the hook refuses Bash commands other than gateway calls. Use roots, or Mode B.
  • A Bash command can rewrite a project's Claude Code settings (for example to set disableAllHooks) unless you ran phiward init in the project: it writes the project settings (phiward install claude --project), whose sandbox entry denies that write. Without it, the hook refuses the plain forms (a redirection, cp, tee, sed -i, git checkout, code that names the file), not a name built from variables or reached after cd .claude. Run phiward init once in each project where you work with protected data (quickstart.md step 3); doctor notes a project without it.
  • The project wiring runs phiward from your PATH. A PATH folder the agent can write (a relative entry, or one inside the project such as node_modules/.bin) could put another program first; keep such entries out of your PATH. User wiring runs phiward by its full path.
  • Credentials that are not files. The macOS Keychain, a Kerberos ticket kept by the macOS credential service (API:) or by the kernel keyring or KCM on Linux (KEYRING:, KCM:), and tokens in your environment cannot be hidden by a file list. Whether a Bash command in Claude Code's sandbox can reach them depends on that sandbox (in the desktop-app test a Keychain-backed GitHub token was not reachable). doctor warns when your tickets are not a file. Mode B blocks the Linux keyring; the macOS Keychain is shared in both modes (launch.md limits).
  • Refusals "above" the hidden list. A Grep or Glob of a folder that holds a hidden path (your home folder, /tmp) is refused, so a session started in the home folder cannot search it; and with a shell that is not sandboxed, ls ~ is refused. Work in a project folder.
  • A session in the home folder. Claude Code's sandbox then lets the shell write your whole home folder, including the places that start programs later (~/.config, ~/.local/bin, ~/Library/LaunchAgents). So phiward counts that shell as not confined: only gateway commands run, and every file-tool write asks you (or is refused where nobody can be asked). The same holds when allowWrite or additionalDirectories names one of those folders. Open Claude Code in a project folder.

That is why Mode B exists. phiward doctor says which mode a session is in and which layers are on.

docs.title: Mode A for a project
docs.text:
The steps are in quickstart.md: each contributor wires Claude Code for every session (phiward setup, or (cd ~ && phiward install claude --user --write)), and runs phiward init once in the project.

Do not rely on project wiring alone. Claude Code loads a project's settings only for a session opened in that folder. A session opened on the folder above it, on another checkout or on a worktree elsewhere gets none of them. doctor warns when only the project is wired.

How the agent knows the rules. install also adds a start-of-session note (a SessionStart hook, phiward session-note claude): every session, in any folder, starts with the rules: protected data only through phiward run and phiward copy, which are the intended route and not a workaround; aggregates only; HPC through phiward run --remote (with your hosts and programs). It names no protected path. A project's own AGENTS.md can say the same for tools that do not run Claude Code's hooks.

docs.title: Wrap an MCP server (Mode A)
docs.text:
An MCP server is a program Claude Code starts, and it runs outside Claude Code's sandbox, with your rights. Start it under phiward launch -- and it runs in phiward's kernel profile, even in a Mode A session: it cannot read protected data or credentials. In your own terminal:

  1. Close Claude Code (it writes ~/.claude.json too).
  2. See what each server is, one line per entry, with its file:
phiward mcp list
  1. Wrap the servers that list offers to wrap (it shows the change and asks first):
phiward mcp wrap NAME

or every one at once: phiward mcp wrap --all. 4. Start Claude Code again: a running session keeps each server as it started it. 5. Check: phiward doctor names any server that still runs with your rights, and any entry whose program Claude Code would look up on a PATH folder the agent can write.

A wrapped entry reads:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "docs": { "command": "/Users/you/.local/share/uv/tools/phiward/bin/phiward",
              "args": ["launch", "--entry", "3f9c2a7b1d4e6a08", "--",
                       "npx", "-y", "some-mcp-server"] }
  }
}

wrap gives each entry an id of its own (--entry): a launcher vouches only for the entry with its id, and an id that two entries hold (a copy) is trusted for neither, so list calls such an entry copied and wrap gives it a new id. An entry wrapped without an id (an older phiward) counts as not wrapped until you run wrap again. wrap writes the full path of the installed launcher, the file phiward's install record lists, in every file, .mcp.json too. Only that file by that path counts as wrapped: phiward by name does not, since Claude Code looks a name up on its PATH, where a project's .venv/bin or node_modules/.bin could supply another phiward, which it would start with your rights. If you commit .mcp.json, a contributor whose phiward is elsewhere runs phiward mcp wrap again; list names an entry whose launcher is by name or another file, and wrap gives it the path. (A source checkout has no install record: there the launcher is the phiward found in the PATH folders the agent cannot write.) It keeps its backups only in its own folder, ~/.phiward/backups/<file>-<hash>/, which the agent cannot write: original (the file before phiward first changed it, never overwritten) and last (before the latest change). Nothing is written beside the config file. phiward mcp unwrap NAME undoes it.

What list may say about a server, and what to do:

list says means do wrapped runs in the kernel profile nothing remote runs on another machine, nothing here nothing not wrapped (runs with your rights) a local command phiward mcp wrap NAME not wrapped: wrapped, but its entry sets a cwd or an env key that changes what runs remove it from the entry: for cwd, give the server absolute paths; for env PATH, name the command by its full path not wrapped: its entry id is also in another entry a copy: their launchers cannot be told apart phiward mcp wrap NAME (a new id) not wrapped: it was wrapped without an entry id an older phiward wrote it phiward mcp wrap NAME not wrapped: it names phiward without its path a folder on PATH the agent can write could supply another launcher phiward mcp wrap NAME (writes the full path) not wrapped: its phiward is not the installed launcher the entry names another phiward file phiward mcp wrap NAME not wrapped: its phiward launch has no -- and a program the entry is malformed fix the entry not wrapped: it has options before -- that wrapped entries do not take --tool, --memory or --report in a launcher entry phiward mcp wrap NAME (drops them, and says so) not wrapped: it starts phiward through uvx, env, uv run, pipx run or Python with -m phiward in front of the launcher: what their words mean differs, so wrap does not rewrite it edit the entry so its command is the server program itself, then phiward mcp wrap NAME listens on this machine / no command phiward can read phiward cannot wrap it its command tools may make only gateway calls

Know that: - phiward must be installed with an install record (uv tool install), or the server needs PHIWARD_DEV=1; - launch makes a .claude folder in the project if there is none; - the env keys of the MCP config reach the server only if [launch] pass_env lists them, and that setting passes them to every launch session, the agent's included; - on macOS, when Claude Code stops the server, only the launcher gets the signal: a server that does not stop at the end of its input keeps running; - plugin and managed MCP servers, and the app's own, are not wrapped this way (wrap does not change a plugin's files: an update replaces them); their tools that run commands may make only gateway calls; - under Mode B (the whole session in phiward launch) a wrapped server's launcher runs inside the session's profile, and the hook treats its command tools the same way (the server is confined there anyway).

How the hook tells which tools are confined: configuration.md; how it trusts a wrapped server: threat-model.md.

Next: the quick start for Mode A, or launch.md for Mode B.

docs.title: The Claude Code plugin, and other plugins
docs.text: For: people who use phiward's Claude Code plugin, or other plugins beside it.

docs.title: phiward's plugin
docs.text:
phiward's repository is also a Claude Code plugin marketplace. The plugin gives a session: - phiward's hooks: the guard on every tool call, and the start-of-session note with the rules; - the skill: how to work through the gateway; - three commands: /phiward:setup (the guided first setup), /phiward:doctor (checks the setup and explains each warning) and /phiward:help (how to work with protected data and HPC); - an MCP server, phiward, whose tools are the gateway: phiward_run, phiward_copy, phiward_remote, phiward_check and phiward_doctor. They do the same checks and masking as the commands, with arguments as lists and no shell.

Tested in a desktop-app session on made-up data: the note, the refusals, the commands and normal work.

The plugin does not install the phiward package, and it cannot set Claude Code's sandbox or permission rules. Those come from the quick start (phiward install claude --user), and they are what stops the reads in a normal session. Keep that user wiring even when you use the plugin: a project can turn a plugin off, but not your user wiring.

docs.title: Install it
docs.text:
In Claude Code, two commands:

/plugin marketplace add msk-access/phiward#v0.2.0b1

/plugin install phiward@phiward

#v0.2.0b1 pins the plugin to the release you installed with uv, so their versions agree. In a terminal, the same is claude plugin marketplace add msk-access/phiward#v0.2.0b1, then claude plugin install phiward@phiward.

docs.title: Offer it to every contributor of a project
docs.text:
The project's committed .claude/settings.json can offer it:

{
  "extraKnownMarketplaces": {
    "phiward": { "source": { "source": "github", "repo": "msk-access/phiward",
                             "ref": "v0.2.0b1" } }
  },
  "enabledPlugins": { "phiward@phiward": true }
}

Each contributor then trusts the folder and installs it (/plugin install phiward@phiward, or claude plugin install phiward@phiward --scope project).

docs.title: Know this
docs.text:
• The plugin runs phiward from the app's PATH. If the desktop app does not find it, every tool call is refused, with a message that says phiward is not installed: quit the app and open it again (quickstart.md). A PATH folder the agent can write could put another program first (modes.md). The user wiring uses the full path.
  • A project can turn a plugin off ("phiward@phiward": false in its settings), unless your organization's managed settings force it on. Your user wiring cannot be turned off by a project that way. A project's disableAllHooks can still turn all hooks off; only managed settings stop that. phiward doctor warns when a project turns the plugin off or sets PATH.
  • For an organization, managed settings are the strong form. They can force the plugin on, allow only managed and forced hooks, and set the sandbox and permission rules.
  • The plugin follows the tag you added. With #v0.2.0b1, the marketplace takes the plugin from that release. Without a tag it follows the repository's main branch. The plugin's version must match the installed phiward package (phiward --version). To move to a new release, update both: uv tool install --force phiward==<version>, then add the marketplace again with the new tag.

docs.title: Other plugins (for example ECC)
docs.text: You can use phiward together with other Claude Code plugins, for example ECC. You do not have to choose. Tested: the phiward plugin and ECC 2.2.3 in one desktop-app session on made-up data. phiward's guard refused the reads of the protected folder, and the normal work ran.

docs.title: How they work together
docs.text:
• Claude Code runs every hook that matches a tool call. phiward's guard runs on each call, whatever other plugins also run. If one hook refuses a call, the call does not run.
  • Other plugins' switches do not turn phiward off. For example, ECC's ECC_HOOKS_ENABLED, ECC_HOOK_PROFILE, ECC_DISABLED_HOOKS and ECC_GATEGUARD=off change only ECC's own hooks.
  • Do not put phiward's guard into another plugin's hook list. Keep phiward as its own plugin, or wire it with phiward install claude --user. The switches of the other plugin could then turn the guard off.
  • The hook is not the protection by itself. In a normal session (Mode A), Claude Code's sandbox and permission rules stop the reads. phiward install claude writes them; no plugin can (modes.md). Under phiward launch (Mode B), the kernel profile stops them.

docs.title: Set up
docs.text:
1. Do the quick start: install phiward, write your config, wire Claude Code and start the broker.
  2. Optional: add the phiward plugin (above).
  3. Install the other plugin as its own instructions tell you.
  4. Run phiward doctor and open a new session.

docs.title: Know this
docs.text:
• In a normal session, other plugins' hooks and MCP servers run as you, outside Claude Code's sandbox. They are not confined by phiward. A hook can read any file that you can read, and it can add text to what Claude Code sends to the model. Install only plugins you trust, and check what their hooks read and keep. Under phiward launch, they run inside the kernel profile, the same as the tool.
  • A hook sees each tool call. A hook that runs before a call sees its input, also when phiward refuses the call: for example a command that names a protected path. A hook that runs after a call also sees its output. Output from phiward run is masked before Claude Code receives it, so a hook sees the masked output.
  • Some plugins stop the agent's first command and ask it questions. For example, ECC's GateGuard asks the agent to state facts before its first shell command, and its message tells the agent how to turn GateGuard off. That is ECC's decision about ECC's own hook. phiward's refusals tell the agent the approved route; they never tell it how to turn a guard off.
  • Under phiward launch, a plugin is not there until you carry it over. Each session starts from a trusted copy of the tool's config (phiward carryover add, see launch.md). A plugin that a session installs or turns on goes to quarantine. Carrying over a plugin such as ECC into launch is not tested yet.

Next: daily use.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
• For: anyone who sets phiward up for the first time.
  • Before: macOS or Linux, and Claude Code 2.1.295 or newer.
  • You will have: phiward installed, your protected folders set, Claude Code wired, and a test that shows it works.
Step Where What you type You see 1. Install Terminal uv tool install ... phiward==0.2.0b1 phiward --version prints the version 2. Set up Terminal (or the plugin) cd ~ && phiward setup its questions, then the config it wrote 3. Check the project folder phiward init, then phiward doctor no PROBLEM or WARNING line

phiward keeps protected data (for example patient data) and your credentials out of what an AI coding agent sends to its model provider. The agent works on protected data only through phiward's gateway (phiward run, phiward copy). A broker runs those commands outside the agent and masks their output. Words in bold are explained in the glossary.

What you get with the steps below: Mode A. The wiring in your user settings covers every Claude Code session, in every folder: phiward's hook checks each tool call, and Claude Code's sandbox keeps shell commands out of your protected folders. In each project where you work with protected data, you also run phiward init once (step 3): without it, a shell command in that project could rewrite the project's Claude Code settings. This is the right start for most people. The stronger Mode B (phiward launch) is for the terminal only; see modes.md when you need it.

docs.title: 1. Install phiward
docs.text:
In Terminal:

curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh

uv tool install --python-preference only-managed phiward==0.2.0b1

uv tool update-shell

The first command installs uv, a Python installer that needs no admin rights. If you have Homebrew, brew install uv does the same. The second gives phiward a Python of its own, which uv downloads once (not Xcode's, conda's or the system's, which another account or tool can change). The last command puts ~/.local/bin, where phiward now is, on your PATH.

Then open a new Terminal, and quit and reopen the Claude Code desktop app (Cmd-Q), so that both find phiward. In the new Terminal, phiward --version prints the version.

On Linux, install bubblewrap and socat first (phiward's kernel profile and Claude Code's sandbox need them), with your package manager, for example sudo apt install bubblewrap socat. Without admin rights, see hpc.md.

Do not install phiward into conda or another shared Python environment: phiward protects its own folder from the agent. Setup also makes phiward's own Python writable by you alone (it says which folders it changed); it never changes your home folder. If an older phiward is in conda, remove it there first (pip uninstall phiward).

docs.title: 2. Set it up
docs.text: Choose one way. Both do the same steps.

docs.title: With Claude Code's help
docs.text:
In a Claude Code session, type these two commands:

/plugin marketplace add msk-access/phiward#v0.2.0b1

/plugin install phiward@phiward

Then open a new session and type:

/phiward:setup

The agent walks you through the steps, and Claude Code asks you before each command. It asks you which folders hold protected data; it never looks into your folders to guess.

It recommends that you write the config yourself, with the two commands of "By hand" below, which it gives you. It can also write the first config for you, while none exists. That is quicker, but then you trust the agent, in that session, to write exactly what you say: do it only in a new session that has not read web pages, other people's files or repositories you do not know. After the first config, only you can change it, in your own Terminal (phiward setup).

If the agent wrote the first config, it holds your protected folders (and copy remotes) only: no results folder, no list of programs, no network. The rest is yours, in your own Terminal: cd ~ && phiward setup, and choose 1 (the steps below). It adds the results folder and the program list, wires Claude Code and starts the broker at every login. More about the plugin: plugins.md.

docs.title: By hand
docs.text:
In Terminal, in your home folder (not inside a project), from a Terminal where your tools (for example samtools from conda) are found:

cd ~ && phiward setup

It asks how you will use phiward. Choose 1, real patient data (the default), and it sets safe defaults for you: - your protected folders (you type them); - a results folder inside the first one, where gateway commands write (Enter accepts it); - a list of programs that gateway commands may run on the data (@genomics), plus a folder of your own scripts if you have one; - no network for gateway commands; - shell commands in Claude Code reach only the hosts you list (Enter says yes). git push and pip install from a session fail until you list their hosts, such as github.com; - which rules mask subject and sample IDs inside your files: none (type 1; there is no default), the msk example pack, or your own patterns; - if you use an HPC cluster: its short name, login host, your user name and work folder. setup writes phiward's ssh config and prints the lines to add to your ~/.ssh/config.

At the end it shows the whole config. Nothing is written until you say yes; then it writes the config and records the folders it protects with your roots (phiward pin). Then it asks three more questions:

  1. "Approve these N program(s) as they are now?" It first lists each program of your program list with its path. The broker runs only the programs you approve. On a first run, with nothing marked, Enter says yes. When a program is marked (changed), or a program in your home folder hides a system program of the same name ((shadows /usr/bin/NAME)), the default is No: read those lines first.
  2. Wire Claude Code for every session? One yes: it shows the change to your user settings (a long list: every protected path and credential, twice) and writes it ((cd ~ && phiward install claude --user --write)).
  3. Start the broker at every login? (A system without a service manager for your login, such as a container or WSL without systemd, cannot: setup says so, and you run phiward broker yourself in a terminal that stays open.)

Say yes to each. The wiring ends with an alias claude='claude --settings ...' line. Add it to your shell startup file (for example ~/.zshrc) yourself, if you start claude in Terminal: then a repository's settings cannot turn the sandbox off. Without it phiward still works; the hook checks the project's settings itself (setup.md). (Choose 2 to try phiward on made-up data with open defaults, or 3 to choose every setting.)

When you change your config later, run (cd ~ && phiward setup) again: it restarts the broker for you. After a change by hand, restart it yourself: the broker refuses requests after the config changes, and the refusal names the command.

A team can share its settings in a template: phiward setup --from team.toml fills in the program list, packs and HPC hosts; each person adds their own folders.

docs.title: 3. Set up each project, and check it
docs.text:
In Terminal, in each project folder where you work with protected data, run once:

phiward init

It only adds; it changes nothing that is there. It adds the phiward rules for agents to AGENTS.md, a .gitignore line, the project's Claude Code settings (.claude/settings.json and .claude/settings.local.json) and git hooks. The project settings stop a shell command from rewriting them. In a repository that is not yours, do not commit these files: list the new ones in .git/info/exclude (for example AGENTS.md and .claude/). Then, in the same folder:

phiward doctor

When all is well, you see lines such as:

protected roots: 1, patterns: 0
  sandbox confines the shell: yes
broker: running

Fix each WARNING; each one says how. A NOTE is for your information. Before Claude Code is wired, one line gives the next step; phiward doctor --verbose lists every check. Then open a new Claude Code session in that folder and ask the agent to read a file in a protected folder: it must be refused. Then ask it to run phiward run -- wc -l <that file>: you get a line count, with the file name masked. (If you said No to the login service, start the broker first: phiward broker in a Terminal of its own.)

If you chose 2 or 3 and now use real patient data, list the programs that gateway commands may run ([broker] commands, see configuration.md): run (cd ~ && phiward setup) again and choose 1.

Next: daily-use.md tells you how to work with the agent on protected data.

docs.title: A project where every contributor is protected
docs.text:
1. Each contributor does steps 1 to 3 above.
  2. Someone runs, once, in the project folder:
phiward init --root data/protected

--root names the project's own protected folders, if it has any. init only adds; it changes nothing that is there. It adds: - the phiward rules for agents to AGENTS.md; - the protected folders to .phiward.toml; - the project's Claude Code settings: the shared part in .claude/settings.json, the personal part in .claude/settings.local.json; - a .gitignore line for the personal file; - git hooks that refuse commits holding protected names or identifiers. 3. Commit AGENTS.md, .phiward.toml, .gitignore and .claude/settings.json. Never commit .claude/settings.local.json. 4. Each other contributor runs phiward init once too (for the personal file and the git hooks), then phiward doctor.

docs.title: HPC
docs.text: The agent never uses ssh itself. It runs approved programs on the cluster with phiward run --remote, and moves files with phiward copy. Both go through your own shared SSH connection, which you open in Terminal (for example kinit, then ssh -fN hpc). No agent request can read your key or Kerberos ticket. The one-time setup is in hpc.md.

docs.title: If something goes wrong
docs.text: What you see What to do Every tool call is refused with "phiward is not installed or not on PATH" The app does not find phiward. Quit the app (Cmd-Q) and open it again. If that does not help, check in Terminal that command -v phiward prints ~/.local/bin/phiward, and run uv tool update-shell again. phiward run says no broker is running Start it at every login: (cd ~ && phiward broker --service --write) in Terminal. Or run phiward broker in a Terminal and keep it open. A command the agent needs is refused The refusal says what to run instead. See daily-use.md. phiward doctor shows a PROBLEM Fix it before you use the agent; the line says how. A wrapped MCP server "failed to connect", or doctor says phiward's own files fail its self-check Usually after uv tool upgrade with umask 002: run (cd ~ && phiward install claude --user --write) again (it makes phiward's own Python writable by you alone), then start Claude Code again. The WARNING names any other step.

docs.title: Releasing phiward
docs.text: For maintainers. A release is a git tag; the release workflow builds the package, checks it, and publishes it to PyPI. No PyPI token is stored anywhere: PyPI trusts the workflow through trusted publishing (OpenID Connect).

docs.title: Once: connect PyPI to the repository
docs.text:
As an owner of the msk-access PyPI account, in a browser: on PyPI, open Your account → Publishing → Add a new pending publisher (for the first release; after that, the project's own Settings → Publishing), and enter: - PyPI project name: phiward - Owner: msk-access - Repository name: phiward - Workflow name: release.yml - Environment name: leave it empty. The publish job runs in no GitHub environment, as in gbcms and krewlyzer: a pushed tag publishes once the tests and checks pass.

A pending publisher does not reserve the name: the first publish creates the project. So publish the first release before the repository is public: until then, anyone could take the name, and the install line in these docs would install their package. Trusted publishing works from a private repository.

docs.title: The first release
docs.text:
1. Create msk-access/phiward as a private repository and push main and develop.
  2. Add the pending publisher (above).
  3. Push the tag (below). The workflow tests, builds and publishes.
  4. Check https://pypi.org/project/phiward/ and the install line.
  5. Only then make the repository public, and turn on GitHub Pages: Settings, Pages, Deploy from a branch, gh-pages, / (root). The docs workflow publishes there with mike: develop as dev, each release tag as its version with the alias stable, which the site opens on.

docs.title: Each release
docs.text:
The repository uses git-flow (gitflow.prefix.versiontag is v): start with git flow release start 0.2.0b2 from develop, make the changes below on that branch, and git flow release finish 0.2.0b2 merges it into main and develop and makes the tag v0.2.0b2. Then push main, develop and the tag.

  1. Set the version: __version__ in src/phiward/__init__.py (the package and phiward --version take it from there), and the same in plugin/.claude-plugin/plugin.json and .claude-plugin/marketplace.json. A test fails when they disagree, and the workflow refuses a tag that names another version. PyPI's form has no v: 0.2.0b1; the tag has it: v0.2.0b1. Change the install lines in the docs (phiward==0.2.0b1) too.
  2. In CHANGELOG.md, replace "unreleased" with the date (UTC), and write the release notes in docs/release-notes/.
  3. Run the full test suite on macOS (tests/README.md says how) and on Linux (sh scripts/linux-check/check.sh, needs Docker: Python 3.12 and 3.9, two layouts, on a git archive of HEAD), and the quickstart in clean Linux containers (sh scripts/quickstart-check/check.sh, needs Docker; its image is built fresh, and --quick runs four plain runs on the cached one while you work): a new user's steps, with umask 022 and 002, must end with no doctor WARNING and a wrapped MCP server. On macOS, run sh scripts/quickstart-check/mac.sh WHEEL PYTHON with uv's or Homebrew's python3 (a home folder of its own, no login service). Then check that the real Claude Code obeys the settings phiward writes, which the scripts above cannot show. You run it yourself, in a terminal: it asks only for a token from claude setup-token, and builds the rest in a home folder of its own, with made-up data. An agent never runs it (it refuses without a terminal, and refuses a token from the environment inside a Claude Code session); an agent runs only sh scripts/sandbox-check/linux.sh --stub.
  4. sh scripts/sandbox-check/check.sh on macOS, and on a real Linux machine with SBX_BASE set (Landlock ABI 2 or newer for the gateway). SBX_BASE holds the check's folders; it may not be under /tmp, the temp folder or your home folder, nor anywhere the settings phiward installs let the session write (the check refuses). On macOS it is /Users/Shared by default; without that folder, set SBX_BASE to another folder outside those (for example one you make for it on a second volume). On a cluster, run it as an interactive job with SBX_BASE on scratch, for example srun --pty --job-name auto-sbx-check env SBX_BASE=/scratch/$USER sh scripts/sandbox-check/check.sh.
  5. sh scripts/sandbox-check/linux.sh on a machine with Docker: the same check in a Linux container, with the Claude Code version that scripts/sandbox-check/docker/package-lock.json pins (CLAUDE_VERSION=2.1.295 builds the lowest version phiward supports instead, unlocked).

Each runs one claude -p session per mode (MODES, default A B; Mode B runs under phiward launch), Haiku with a spending cap of $1 and a time limit. The session must be refused when it reads the protected file with the Read tool, and when a Bash command reads it, writes the data folder, ~/.phiward or ~/.claude/settings.json; phiward run from the session must mask its output, a commit of a made-up identifier must be refused by the git hook without showing it, the wrapped MCP server must start, and doctor must stay clean. It ends with a verdict per mode and an overall PASS, FAIL or INCONCLUSIVE. With REMOTE=HOST REMOTE_DIR=/abs/new/empty/folder (on a real machine), it also pushes, runs, and pulls through your shared connection, which you start when it asks; it writes only under REMOTE_DIR and deletes nothing there: remove that folder yourself afterwards. --stub (a stand-in claude, no token) checks the plumbing only, and runs only in the container (linux.sh --stub): elsewhere check.sh --stub refuses, as it would plant a git hook and a home folder on your machine. (That refusal looks for the container's marks, /.dockerenv or SBX_IMAGE: a tripwire, not a gate.) A token you set in the environment is read once and unset at the start: only the claude process gets it. The check's home folder and its judge's folder are removed at the end, also after Ctrl-C, SIGTERM or a closed terminal; if one cannot be removed, the check names it and exits non-zero. A kill -9 of check.sh or launch.py skips that: the session may keep running, and the folders stay (remove them yourself). Only the report and, per mode, the stream and the facts are kept, redacted in memory: with KEEP=1 in a folder of their own (phiward-sbx-kept-* next to it), and with linux.sh in its output folder. If the token's value is still in any of them, nothing is kept ("redaction failed: nothing kept"). A process the session starts in a session of its own (setsid) can outlive the check; its folders are removed all the same, so nothing it writes is kept. The stream reaches launch.py through a pipe, and launch.py writes it, after the session is stopped, into the judge's folder: next to the home folder, outside the folders the check gives the session. The check does not prove that the sandbox cannot write there; a process left running in a session of its own could, before the judge reads it. On Linux too the wrapped MCP server must start in Mode B: its launch inside the session runs it directly (the session's seccomp fingerprint). A server that does not start leaves the mode INCONCLUSIVE, as on macOS. What the session writes in its project folder (results.txt, server.out) a model could forge, line by line. The checks made outside the session are harder to forge: a probe's file on the host, the settings file's hash, the marker or the token in the stream, and the transcript's tool calls (with the limit above). Read a PASS with that in mind. Run the real check when phiward's Claude Code wiring (install.py, claude_settings.py, fasthook.py, mcp.py, wholetool.py) or the lowest Claude Code version it supports changed since the last release; otherwise skip it. 4. Commit and tag: git flow release finish does both; the first release is tagged by hand on main. Then push the tag:

git tag -a v0.2.0b1 -m "phiward v0.2.0b1"

git push origin v0.2.0b1
  1. The release workflow runs the whole test suite (macOS and Linux, Python 3.9 to 3.14), checks that the tag names the version everywhere, builds the wheel and the source archive, checks them (twine check --strict), installs the wheel and runs it. Only then does the publish job start; nothing waits for an approval, so push the tag only when the release is ready. Its actions are pinned by commit; update a pin by its release's commit, not a tag.
  2. After it is published, check the install line from a clean shell:
uv tool install --python-preference only-managed phiward==0.2.0b1
  1. Make the GitHub release from the tag, with the release notes.

A version on PyPI can be yanked but never replaced: a fix is a new version.

docs.title: Setup reference
docs.text:
For: anyone who wants each setup step, option and limit explained; upgrades; removal.

The quick start is the short way. This page explains each step, its options and its limits, in the same order. Run the steps in your own Terminal. The guided setup (/phiward:setup) lets the agent run the first-time steps for you, but only while no config exists (below).

  1. Check the requirements
  2. Install
  3. Write the user config with phiward setup
  4. Wire the agent tool
  5. Start the broker
  6. Pin the derived folders
  7. Check everything with phiward doctor
  8. Try it on made-up data
  9. Per repository: .phiward.toml and the git hooks

Later: change the setup, upgrade from agent-guards, remove phiward.

docs.title: 1. Requirements
docs.text:
• Python 3.9 or newer.
  • macOS: /usr/bin/sandbox-exec (part of macOS; Apple marks it as deprecated, Claude Code uses it too).
  • Linux:
  • bubblewrap (bwrap) on the PATH;
  • Landlock ABI 2 or newer in the kernel (Linux 5.19 or newer, with Landlock turned on). The gateway uses it as a second layer for its writes and refuses to run without it;
  • on Ubuntu 24.04, AppArmor can block unprivileged user namespaces (kernel.apparmor_restrict_unprivileged_userns). Then bubblewrap cannot start. Change the setting, or add an AppArmor profile for bwrap. doctor says when this is the cause.
  • Native Windows has no confinement. Use WSL 2, which is Linux.
  • For Claude Code: version 2.1.295 or newer (it needs onFailure on hooks). On Linux, Claude Code's own sandbox (Mode A) also needs bubblewrap and socat; install sets failIfUnavailable, so without them Claude Code stops at start instead of running commands unsandboxed. doctor checks both.

Without a working confinement backend, the broker refuses to run anything. It fails closed.

docs.title: 2. Install
docs.text:
Install a release from PyPI with uv (to get uv itself: curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh, or brew install uv):

uv tool install --python-preference only-managed phiward==0.2.0b1

Or with pipx:

pipx install phiward==0.2.0b1

Name the version: a beta is not chosen without it. The same release from its GitHub tag, without PyPI: uv tool install git+https://github.com/msk-access/phiward@v0.2.0b1. Pin a version or a tag; do not install a branch. Use uv tool or pipx: they give phiward a Python folder of its own. phiward protects the folder of the Python that runs it (the agent may not write there, or it could change what the broker runs), so an install into a shared environment (a conda base, a project's .venv) would make that whole environment read-only for the agent. They also keep the launcher at one path across upgrades (~/.local/share/uv/tools/phiward/bin/phiward, pipx's folder, for example ~/.local/share/pipx/venvs/phiward/bin/phiward), which phiward mcp wrap writes into each entry; an install whose path holds the version (phiward in a Homebrew Python's own site folder) would need wrap again after each upgrade. Check the install:

phiward --help

docs.title: 3. The user config: phiward setup
docs.text:
setup first asks how you will use phiward:

  1. Real patient data (the default): you give your protected folders; it suggests a results folder inside the first one (the one write place, so no --write-to is needed), sets the program list to @genomics plus an optional folder of your own scripts, gives gateway commands no network, asks whether shell commands may reach only hosts you list ([network]; yes is suggested; with yes, git push and pip install fail until you list their hosts), and asks about HPC.
  2. Made-up data: your folders and a results folder; any program may run.

Every profile also asks which rules mask subject and sample identifiers (Question 8). 3. Every setting: the questions below, one by one.

phiward setup --from team.toml starts from a team template (a config file with shared settings); its settings fill in what your config does not have, and lists are joined with yours. A template may set only shared settings: the program list (by name or @ list, not by path), built-in packs, HPC host names and the programs allowed there, cluster folders to mask, patterns, and limits (only lower than the defaults). It may never set a write place, the network, a copy remote, an ssh config, names files, pack files or environment. One kept in a project (a folder with .git, .claude or .phiward.toml above it) is refused. setup shows every setting in it and asks before it uses them. At the end setup writes the file after your yes, makes the results folder and phiward's ssh config, approves the programs, wires Claude Code, and installs or restarts the broker service (each with a yes; see the end of the dialogue).

The user config holds the facts of your machine: which folders are protected, and what gateway commands may do. Once step 4 is done, the agent's shell cannot write it, and the hook refuses the agent's file tools for its usual spelling (not for every spelling: known gap 2). Write it with:

phiward setup

Each answer is checked as phiward checks the file later; a refused answer is asked again, with the reason. Nothing is written until you say yes at the end. It writes ~/.config/phiward/config.toml (or the file that $PHIWARD_CONFIG names; see configuration.md) with mode 0600, and keeps the old file as config.toml.bak (each run replaces the .bak file, so copy it away if you want to keep an older one).

Once a config exists, setup is yours only: it refuses to run without a terminal, and the hook refuses it as an agent command. These two checks are a convenience, not a boundary: a program can fake a terminal. What stops an agent is that Claude Code's sandbox (or launch) denies writes to the config, ~/.phiward and the service file. If an agent shows you phiward setup as a command to approve, refuse it.

docs.title: The guided first run
docs.text:
We recommend that you run phiward setup yourself, as above. The guided setup (/phiward:setup) recommends it too, and gives you the commands.

It can also let the agent write the first config: phiward setup --first-run --root PATH [--root PATH ...] [--remote host:/path ...], with the paths that you type in chat. This works only while no config exists. It writes protected roots and copy remotes only (each remote's folder also as a [remote] root, so a push can land there), never a grant (no write places, no network). It refuses a PHIWARD_CONFIG, PHIWARD_SPOOL or XDG_* override without a terminal.

When to use it, and what you trust. Before your config exists, nothing protects the agent's choices: you trust the agent, in that session, to write exactly what you said, and to install the broker service and the wiring as they should be. Use it only in a new session that has not read web pages, other people's files or repositories you do not know. Then check what it wrote: phiward doctor --show-paths, in your own Terminal, lists the roots. These limits hold on both paths: - a root that is your home folder or above it, in a dot-folder of your home folder, in ~/Library or in a PATH folder stays protected, but gateway commands cannot write in it (your own tools load code from there); - a copy remote must name a work folder: not /, a folder just below it, a home folder, or a dot-folder; - the broker service skips PATH folders inside a project, and folders the agent's sandbox may write (a temp folder, also inside your home folder, the spool, an allowWrite folder of your own or the managed settings).

The agent-run setup takes KRB5CCNAME and the other Kerberos variables from its session, as your own shell names them. If your ticket cache is in a place other than the default ones, run the setup yourself.

docs.title: Question 1: protected roots
docs.text:
Folders that hold protected data. Give each one as an absolute path or with ~/, one per line, and an empty line to end the list.

  • Give the folder that holds the data, not a folder above it. A root cannot be /, your home folder, or a folder above your home folder (the agent could not work at all). setup refuses these; the loader refuses only /, so take care when you edit the file by hand.
  • A root cannot hold a phiward file or folder (for example ~/.config, which holds the user config). setup refuses such a root.
  • Each root must exist; setup refuses a missing one. Claude Code's sandbox hides a root only when it exists as a command starts.
  • Prefer the real path. A root reached through a link is protected, but gateway commands cannot write to it (doctor says so).
  • Keep protected data outside the git repositories that the agent works in. The .git folder of a work tree that holds a root is protected too, so the agent cannot use git there.

docs.title: Question 2: protected patterns (optional)
docs.text: Glob patterns, such as /data/runs/*/panel, for protected places that are spread out. * is the only wildcard, and only printable ASCII is accepted (see configuration.md). Prefer roots: Claude Code's sandbox cannot take patterns, so on Linux its shell does not count as confined while patterns are set, and the hook then refuses shell commands other than gateway calls (see configuration.md). The gateway and phiward launch still enforce patterns.

docs.title: Question 3: write places ([broker] write_to)
docs.text:
Folders where phiward run --write-to DIR may write. DIR must be one of these folders or a folder inside one. Use this for result folders, for example ~/projects/study-a/results.

  • Each folder must exist, and you must give its real path (no link on the way). It must not hold a .claude folder: choose a results folder, not a project folder. (A .claude folder made there later makes phiward skip the entry.) setup shows the real path when you give a link.
  • A write place cannot be /, your home folder or above it, in a dot-folder of your home folder (~/.ssh, ~/.config), in ~/Library or a PATH folder, above a protected root, in a derived protected folder or a pattern match, hold a names or pack file of the config, or hold or be inside a phiward file or folder. It may sit inside a protected root: what is written there stays protected.
  • Gateway commands write only in their own scratch folder and in these places: protected roots are read only for them. So a workflow that writes results next to protected data needs a write place inside that root, for example ~/data/patients/derived.
  • Each write place gives code that the agent chooses a place to put what it read. To keep the gateway as closed as possible, keep this list short.

docs.title: Question 4: programs ([broker] commands)
docs.text: The programs gateway commands may run. Empty means any program: then code the agent writes can run on protected data. For real data, list them: @genomics or @counts (built-in lists), program names, your own scripts by full path, or a folder of your scripts as a path ending in /. Interpreters and shells (python3, bash) run any code: list your scripts instead. Choice 1 sets @genomics and asks for a folder of your own scripts; how a script gets there is in daily-use.md.

docs.title: Question 5: network for gateway commands ([broker] net)
docs.text: With yes, phiward run --net gets the network. Code that reads protected data could then send it anywhere. The default and the recommendation is no. phiward copy to a configured remote gets the network for that copy without this setting.

docs.title: Question 6: copy remotes ([copy] remotes)
docs.text:
Places on other machines that phiward copy may copy to or from, as host:/absolute/prefix (through your shared SSH connection: hpc.md). For example cluster:/data/work/study-a. Leave the list empty if you do not copy to another machine. Each remote is a place where protected data may go.

A remote copy does not read ~/.ssh/config (the agent may be able to write it). It reads phiward's own ssh config ([copy] ssh_config), which the HPC questions below write for you; or write a small one yourself and set [copy] ssh_config by hand (configuration.md).

docs.title: Question 7: network for shell commands ([network])
docs.text: With yes, the shell commands an agent runs in Claude Code reach only the hosts you list (Claude Code's own sandbox enforces it). Commands that need the network fail until their hosts are listed: git push needs github.com (or your git server), pip install needs *.pypi.org and files.pythonhosted.org. Claude Code itself, WebFetch and MCP servers are not limited by it. Each listed host is a way out, so list few. Choice 1 asks this too, with yes suggested.

docs.title: Question 8: subject and sample identifiers ([sanitize])
docs.text:
The gateway masks the names of files and folders under your protected roots, and the genomics pack masks sequence file names, read names and loci. A patient, sample or donor ID inside a file, or in a name outside the roots, is masked only by a rule for its form. Choose:

  1. Your data holds no such IDs beyond the names under the roots: setup records subjects = "none". This is never the default: type 1 each time.
  2. The msk pack: one institution's forms. It is an example; copy it for another institution.
  3. Your own rules, one per line ([sanitize] patterns), each checked as you type it.

Every profile asks this (in choice 3 it is numbered 8). Setup keeps genomics in any pack list it writes, also on a re-run over a list you wrote without it. Until one of these is set, phiward doctor warns.

docs.title: The HPC questions
docs.text: Choices 1 and 3 then ask whether you work with an HPC cluster. With yes, they ask for its short name, its login host, your user name and work folder there, and the cluster folders to mask. setup adds the work folder to the copy remotes, writes phiward's ssh config and prints the lines to add to your own ~/.ssh/config (hpc.md).

docs.title: The end of the dialogue
docs.text:
1. setup shows the whole new file and the difference from the old one, and asks whether to write it.
  2. It pins the derived folders (step 6).
