Left out: the standard library's own packages link, with that folder. install fixes what the check names of a link inside your home folder (every folder of a chain, the target, that deepest folder), and judges it again after each change. The contents of a linked folder are not walked: anyone who could plant such a link could change the standard library itself, which is not hashed either. - A check that runs inside the code it checks cannot stop an account that changed that code first; that is why install makes the files safe and doctor checks them all. - Not checked: ACLs (mode bits do not show them, on macOS or NFSv4), and dynamic libraries loaded from elsewhere (for example Homebrew's OpenSSL). - What Claude Code protects by itself: its sandbox keeps commands from writing "most of" ~/.claude (or $CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR), ~/.claude.json and the credentials file, even under an allowWrite that covers them. The docs give no exact list and no version for it. phiward refuses the settings that the docs say remove this protection (filesystem.disabled, allowNestedUserNamespaces), and adds nothing of its own there. On Linux a denyWrite path that does not exist yet becomes a read-only placeholder file, which could block a plugin install. - Scripts that Claude Code settings name (a hook's command, statusLine, apiKeyHelper) run with your full rights. Keep them under a hooks/ folder of ~/.claude or of the project's .claude (the hook asks before a file tool writes there, and Claude Code's sandbox denies its shell), or in a folder no session writes; never elsewhere in a project. - Not tested by phiward's own checks: Claude Code's real sandbox. The test suite never runs the real claude. The release check (scripts/sandbox-check, releasing.md) does, on macOS and Linux, run by the operator: one session per mode, judged from its files. Its probe lines are written inside the session, so a model could forge them; the checks made outside it (files on the host, the settings hash, the stream that launch.py writes after the session) are harder to forge, but a process the session leaves running could still reach them before the judge reads them. It does not cover MCP tools, WebFetch, IDEs on Linux, remote with use_shared_connection = false, RHEL 8, NFS home folders, sssd or Kerberos; and the first check after your own install is yours. - The spool folder is writable by the agent: it can fill it or move it, which stops the gateway (the broker stops when its folder is moved). It cannot make the broker write outside the folder or run a command through a shell. - The broker's status file only adds protection to the agent's side. On Linux, if it does not exist when an agent shell starts, that shell can create it in its way; the agent's own config still applies, and doctor reports a mismatch. - The gateway is not a container. It sees the whole file system read-only, the roots included; it writes only to the places listed above.

docs.title: Gaps of the hook alone
docs.text:
These apply when only phiward's hook runs, without Claude Code's sandbox (Mode A) or launch (Mode B). Each gap was found by a review. Confirmed means a probe on made-up data showed it; not verified or from reading the code means it was not shown by a probe.

The agent tool itself 1. File tools are checked by path, then used by path. A link swapped in between can give a Read the content of a protected file (confirmed by a simulation, not through Claude Code). Spellings the hook does not resolve also pass it: /.vol/<dev>/<inode>/... and /System/Volumes/Data/... on macOS (confirmed), and accented names in the other Unicode form (confirmed). 2. The hook's list of files the agent may not write is incomplete. It refuses file-tool writes to phiward's own files (compared as the file system compares names, and by device and inode), and to Claude Code's settings*.json, .mcp.json and ~/.claude.json. It asks before a file tool writes what Claude Code runs as code (hooks, skills, plugins: rule 2 above). It cannot know every file another tool runs later. In Mode A, Claude Code's own permission rules (install writes Edit deny rules for phiward's files) and its sandbox cover more. 3. MCP servers and the tool's hooks run outside the kernel profile. A local MCP server runs with your rights unless it is wrapped in phiward launch --. The hook sees only what a tool is asked to do, never what it returns. So a tool that returns your terminal text or a file can show protected data. A published server (@modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem 2.3.0) wrapped this way read ordinary files and could neither read nor list a protected folder (Linux; confirmed).

The agent's confined shell (Claude Code's sandbox) 4. It can write files the operator or a later unconfined tool runs: shell startup files, ~/.ssh/config, ~/.gitconfig, .git/config and .git/hooks, LaunchAgents, programs in PATH folders, ~/.claude.json (user-scope MCP servers), ~/.claude/hooks, plugins, .mcp.json. Under Claude Code's sandbox, writes are limited to its allowed folders (the project, the temporary folder, the broker's spool). Claude Code's documentation says the sandbox also denies writes to .claude settings files and .mcp.json in the working folder and the folders above it, shell startup files, .gitconfig and .git/hooks and .git/config in the working folder, and most of ~/.claude. phiward's HPC probe confirmed this for the sandbox engine with explicit entries, not for Claude Code's own list. 5. Keystroke injection: from a confined shell, a program can queue keystrokes into the terminal that started it (TIOCSTI; confirmed under a profile like phiward's old one, not tested under Claude Code's own sandbox). 6. Unconfined programs it can reach, unless the sandbox blocks them: unix sockets (tmux, ssh connection sharing, ssh-agent, systemd, job schedulers), IDE extensions, open / LaunchServices, Spotlight (mdfind), Claude in Chrome (from the reviews; a unix-socket server was confirmed, the others not verified). 7. Pattern forms the kernel does not enforce: a ? or [...] that must match a non-ASCII character, and some class forms ([!-x], ranges across /) (confirmed). Use roots, or patterns with * and ASCII names only. 8. A root spelled /System/Volumes/Data/... in the config is not denied by Seatbelt on its normal path (confirmed). Write roots in their normal form. 9. Other names of a protected file: an existing hard link outside a root is readable (confirmed on macOS). On macOS, other mounts of the same data are not detected: list each mount path as a root. On Linux, other mounts of the same file system are not covered by the hook alone, and a guard file that does not exist yet (for example a user site folder) is not protected (from reading the code).

The trusted side (broker, hook, doctor, install, git hooks) 10. The base Python that phiward runs on is not a guard folder (with uv, Homebrew, pyenv or conda it is user-writable) (confirmed). 11. doctor's self-test runs true found on PATH without a restriction (confirmed). 12. install --project --write writes its backup and temporary file through links that may be planted in the project (confirmed). 13. The git hook's fallback (python3 -m phiward) can import a planted package from the repository (confirmed). 14. Programs and their settings: Linux finds bwrap on PATH (confirmed); a remote copy's rsync reads ~/.popt on Linux (confirmed in Docker); an operator ssh_config may Include or Match exec files the agent can write, and ssh reads ~/.ssh/known_hosts and id_* (from reading the code). 15. The start environment of the broker, doctor and setup comes from the operator's shell startup files (see gap 4) (from reading the code).

On a cluster 16. Job submission (sbatch, srun) from the agent's shell runs jobs outside any profile, on nodes that see the same data (from reading the design; not probed). 16b. Protection follows the path (confirmed on Linux, by design on macOS): a protected folder that the operator moves outside its protected path, into a folder a session can see, is readable there, during a session or after it.

Smaller path and trusted-side gaps 17. Each smaller, all real: - grant checks compare paths as raw text, so a case twin of ~/.ssh or of a root's parent passes the write_to check (confirmed); - a root written in NFD Unicode form is not masked by the sanitizer (confirmed); - entry names that are not valid UTF-8 are not masked on Linux (confirmed); - a .git file (worktree, submodule) makes the gitfile, not the real object store, the derived root (from reading the code); - Claude Code settings are read following links and can block on a FIFO; the "confined" relaxation trusts project settings that phiward does not deny; - the plugin's and install --project's hooks run the first phiward found on PATH (the user wiring names phiward's own Python by its full path); - git is found on PATH, and the pre-commit hook runs git diff without --no-textconv, with core.fsmonitor and core.hooksPath read from the repository; - with a pip --user install, the launcher folder is on sys.path; - user pack files and names_from files outside the roots are not guard files, so masking can be weakened.

docs.title: Reduce the risk (every mode)
docs.text:
1. If the agent reads untrusted input (web pages, issues, other people's repositories, MCP tools), use Mode B (phiward launch), or run it as a separate user, or on a machine, with no protected data.
  2. Install phiward with uv tool or pipx, and keep its Python out of the agent's reach.
  3. Prefer roots; in patterns use only * and ASCII names. Write roots in their normal form (not /System/Volumes/Data/...). Avoid hard links and second mounts of protected data.
  4. Give no write places, no network and no copy remotes unless you need them; keep write places away from project folders.
  5. Use only MCP servers, plugins and hooks you trust.
  6. Run install --project only in a project you created.
  7. Run the agent in a terminal that holds nothing else; do not leave tmux, ssh connection sharing, ssh-agent or other socket services open to it.
  8. Do not run agents on a cluster login node that can submit jobs against protected data.
  9. After agent sessions, review: shell startup files, ~/.ssh/config, ~/.gitconfig, .git/config and .git/hooks, LaunchAgents, programs in PATH folders, ~/.claude.json, ~/.claude/hooks, ~/.claude/plugins, and the project's .claude/ and .mcp.json.

docs.title: Mode A: a Claude Code session
docs.text:
phiward install claude wires the session. Bash (and Monitor) runs in Claude Code's own sandbox, which denies protected roots and the hidden list. The file tools are refused them by phiward's hook and by Claude Code's permission deny rules (both resolve links). A start-of-session note tells the agent the rules. Tested in the desktop app: reads of protected data and of a made-up credential by the Read tool and by cat were refused, ssh to HPC failed, a Keychain-backed GitHub token was not reachable from the session's Bash, and ordinary work was unaffected. What it does not do:

  • the file tools are refused inside Claude Code, not by the kernel: a spelling that both the permission rules and the hook miss reads the file;
  • hooks and MCP servers that are not wrapped in phiward launch -- run with your rights;
  • credentials that are not files (the macOS Keychain in general, Kerberos caches kept by the macOS credential service or the Linux kernel keyring or KCM, tokens in your environment) are not hidden by a file list; doctor warns about ticket caches that are not files;
  • only sessions that load the wiring are protected: project wiring applies only to a session opened in that folder; wire your user settings (--user) so every session is covered;
  • a repository can turn the phiward plugin off unless managed settings force it on;
  • a gateway command may write files that run later (.git/hooks, .mcp.json, .envrc) inside a write_to folder or a copy's destination; give write_to folders that are not projects, and read what lands there before you run anything from it. Protected roots themselves are read only for the gateway;
  • on Linux, a run --write-to command can write a .claude folder below the top of its write_to folder (bubblewrap makes only the top one read only); do not open a Claude Code session inside a write_to folder;
  • the hook reads the config that its environment names (HOME, PHIWARD_CONFIG, XDG_CONFIG_HOME, CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR and the spool and cache variables). A project whose settings set a PHIWARD_* variable in env (a repository you clone can) makes the hook refuse every tool call, and doctor names it. Claude Code ignores HOME, XDG_* and CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR there. Claude Code's sandbox and the hook refuse Bash and file-tool writes to those settings. The hook does not check its config against the broker's;
  • another session's gateway replies in the spool can be changed by the agent (it is the same user): a forged reply leaks nothing, but it can mislead you or another agent;
  • the first setup: before your config exists, nothing protects it. If the agent writes the first config (/phiward:setup, setup --first-run), you trust that session to write what you said; see setup.md.

docs.title: How the hook trusts a wrapped MCP server
docs.text:
Claude Code starts a server when a session starts and keeps it running. So a server wrapped in the config afterwards still runs bare. After phiward mcp wrap, start Claude Code again; /resume, /clear and compaction change nothing.

Which server a tool belongs to. The hook learns it from Claude Code itself (mcp_server.source, 2.1.274 and newer; Claude Code's docs say to base trust on it, not on the name). It reads that one scope's entry: .claude.json or .mcp.json, or a plugin's installed files. The agent cannot write .claude.json or .mcp.json: the file tools refuse them, and the sandbox denies them to Bash. The app's own servers (sdk) and every source phiward does not read count as bare. So a repository's .mcp.json cannot speak for a server of the app's that has the same name. Without a source (an older Claude Code, Copilot) only ~/.claude.json counts and .mcp.json servers are bare. A config file that cannot be read strictly makes its scope bare. A config entry phiward cannot read (args that is not a list of strings) counts as bare, and does not change how the others are read.

The record. Each phiward launch keeps a record of its own process in ~/.phiward/launched while it runs: process id, start time, parent, a hash of what it runs (its command), and a hash of what its profile hides (the hidden list, the roots and the patterns). It is a guard folder: the agent cannot write it, its confined server can read it but not write it, and neither it nor ~/.phiward may be a link. The hook trusts a wrapped entry only while a live launcher of its command is a child of the hook's own Claude Code. A launcher the agent starts from Bash has the sandboxed shell as its parent, never an ancestor of the hook. The hook takes the nearest of its own ancestors (up to four) with launcher children as its Claude Code. So a Claude Code started inside another's Bash is best effort (its environment is the agent's). The hook also trusts a record only when its profile hash is the one the hook would build itself. An entry counts as bare when its env changes the hidden list (KRB5CCNAME, KRB5_CONFIG), or when the config or your credentials changed since the server started. It stays bare until Claude Code starts it again.

Inside launch (Mode B). The record folder is a guard folder in Mode B too, so a wrapped server's launcher inside the session cannot write its record (record_launch gives up quietly), and the hook keeps that server bare. It is not made writable: a record the session can write, it can forge. This matters only for an MCP tool with a shell-like name under a * matcher: the hook that launch writes matches the file tools and Bash only, and the kernel profile confines the server. A launch inside the session runs its command directly, under the session's profile (on Linux it knows it is inside from the session's seccomp filter); that profile is wider than a server's own (SERVER_READ_ONLY), as on macOS. Any launch inside a session runs so, also for another project: that project's repo config (.phiward.toml) is not applied. Any process may install such a filter on itself and its children, so the fingerprint is not a secret: forging it needs code running in the launcher or one of its ancestors, and such code could skip launch anyway.

Plugins and configured servers. A launcher also notes a hash of its CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT, which Claude Code exports only to a plugin's stdio server. - A configured server needs a launcher without one, started with its entry's own id (phiward launch --entry ID, which wrap writes). That id is its launch hash. So one launcher never vouches for two entries, and no entry is parsed for what else it might start. An id found twice, anywhere in the config files' strings, is trusted for nothing (decoded JSON: a copy of the entry, in any wrapper, makes both untrusted). - A plugin's server needs a launcher of its own copy's folder (any copy that applies to this project). A plugin's launcher counts only for that plugin's copy, never for a configured server. So a plugin never vouches for your server, and a broken or disabled plugin does not affect it. A plugin's entries carry no ids (the plugin's author writes them). There the hook counts every entry of the copy that may start a launcher with the command, also through nice, env or a shell's -c text (every launch word, split at ;, && and |). Counting too many only asks for more launchers. - A launcher with any CLAUDE_PLUGIN_* variable but no plugin folder is trusted for nothing. If Claude Code itself was started with a CLAUDE_PLUGIN_* variable set, its configured servers' launchers carry it and are not trusted. A configured entry whose env sets CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT or CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA counts as bare.

How an entry is compared. Folders are compared as they really lead. A plugin's entry is filled in exactly as Claude Code fills it (checked with Claude Code 2.1.318): the folder as the registry has it, the data folder without a trailing /. Its ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA} is filled in as ~/.claude/plugins/data/<id>. A launcher of another fill does not count. A configured entry's placeholders are filled in without the hook's own plugin variables. An entry whose command holds ${VAR} is compared as the hook fills it in, and a mismatch counts as bare. The launcher itself counts only when the entry's command is, by its full path, the launcher phiward's install record lists (a guard file). phiward by name never counts, since Claude Code looks it up on its own PATH when it starts the server. A source checkout has no record. There the launcher is the phiward found in the PATH folders the agent cannot write (the broker's rule, and none inside $CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR).

Why the records are safe. Claude Code's sandbox denies all of ~/.phiward to Bash, after phiward install claude --write writes it into denyWrite. Until then doctor says the shell is not confined, and the hook refuses shell commands other than gateway calls. The shell counts as confined only with that entry, and with no allowWrite that re-opens part of it. denyWrite holds inside writable folders. So neither a session opened in the home folder, nor --add-dir ~, nor an allowWrite can write, rename or replace the records or wrap's backups. phiward mcp wrap keeps its backups only in ~/.phiward/backups, a guard folder: nothing beside a config file is ever shown as the operator's original. The spool, the one folder the agent must write, lives outside it (~/.phiward-spool). install makes the folders up front. So bubblewrap, which protects only paths that exist, covers them from the first session on.

A server reached by URL counts as remote only when the URL surely names another machine. The URL must be plain ASCII with no \, no user part and no % in the host. The host must not be this machine: 127.0.0.1 in any spelling, 0177.1, [::1], [::ffff:127.0.0.1], localhost, *.localhost, a link-local address, this machine's host name, a name /etc/hosts maps to it. Claude Code reads URLs with Node's parser, which accepts many more spellings; any URL phiward cannot read this strictly counts as this machine. A server on this machine (an IDE's) runs outside Claude Code: phiward cannot wrap it (phiward mcp wrap leaves it alone and says so), and its command tools may make only gateway calls. Not recognised: a DNS name that points at this machine, and this machine's own network address (10.x, 192.168.x); such a "remote" server counts as remote.

docs.title: Mode B: phiward launch
docs.text:
phiward launch --tool claude runs the whole agent tool, and every child it starts, in the kernel profile: its file tools, MCP servers and hooks are confined too, so the hook is no longer the guard for them. What changes for the operator:

Files that run later. A coding agent must write in the project, and you later run what is there: tests, builds, scripts, git with its hooks and config, editor tasks, git hook managers (.husky/, lefthook). No sandbox can tell a planted hook from a real change. launch makes the common places read-only (git control files of every repository it finds at start, .claude and .vscode settings, .mcp.json) and, on Linux, reports git control files a session changed, but the class cannot be closed by a list. The rule: treat everything in the project as written by the agent. Run project commands inside launch (phiward launch -- git status, phiward launch -- make test), or read the change before you run it outside.

Known open items in this phase: - the network is open under launch (a proxy for listed hosts is planned; [network] limit covers Mode A's shell commands only). The agent cannot read protected data under launch, so this matters for credentials and for gateway output; - the tool's environment is an allow-list (proxy, CA and locale variables, the tool's own ANTHROPIC_/CLAUDE_ ones); add more with [launch] pass_env in the user config, knowing that whatever you pass is readable by the agent; - macOS: the Keychain stays reachable (Claude Code keeps its own login there); items whose access list trusts security or git credential-osxkeychain can be read; other apps' preferences are readable; - macOS: only the session's own terminal can be read or written. Tools that open new terminals (script, tmux, expect) do not work yet. When xcrun's cache is stale, the /usr/bin tools print a cache warning (the cache is never written under launch). The per-user temp folder is writable (the compiler uses it); - both systems: git control files are covered for the repositories found when launch starts (top, nested, submodules; up to 50,000 entries, skipping node_modules, .venv and similar). Repositories created during a session, nested .claude, .vscode, .mcp.json files and git hook managers (.husky/) are not: see the rule above. .claude/settings.local.json is read-only (it can hold hooks), so Claude Code's "don't ask again" answers do not stay in the project under launch; - Linux: abstract unix sockets are scoped only on kernels with Landlock ABI 6 (a warning says so). Unix sockets made after launch starts, or with relative paths, are not covered. Missing settings files are made as read-only {} placeholders in the project. After a session, launch reports git control files that changed; - HPC through Kerberos and mounts (the operator's setup): a session cannot read the operator's Kerberos ticket caches (the one KRB5CCNAME names, krb5cc* files in the shared temp folders, /run/user/<uid> on Linux), ~/.ssh, the SSH agent, or the shared SSH connection's socket. So the agent cannot log in to HPC itself and read data there unmasked. HPC work goes through the gateway, which the operator's broker runs over the operator's shared SSH connection (hpc.md): phiward run --remote and phiward copy (tested against a real cluster). Protected data on HPC storage mounted on the Mac needs its mount path in the protected roots. - carry-over: each session gets a fresh config folder, built from a trusted copy and thrown away at exit. Nothing is shared between sessions. Instruction changes go to quarantine (phiward carryover show | accept ID, add PATH). Every file the session changed in the project is listed, instructions for models first. Auto memory is off unless --memory. Nothing is ever killed: on macOS a process a session leaves behind keeps running, but what it writes does not reach a later session (tests/test_v2_s17.py, test_18); - a fresh config folder for the tool: your normal Claude Code memory, skills, plugins and MCP servers are not there until you add them (phiward carryover add), and a login token is needed (launch.md).

Recorded limits (beta). These stay open in the beta. Each one belongs to the class "files that run later" or to the macOS process model:

Limit What reduces it L1 macOS: other folders that a later plain run reads as settings (for example a nested .claude) can be made in the project. launch makes .claude at start and refuses to make .vscode, so these two cannot become links. The rule above. L2 Linux: a missing .vscode folder can be made, with files in it. launch makes placeholders only in a .vscode that exists. The rule above. L3 .claude/settings.local.json is read-only, but a plain run outside launch still reads whatever was in it before the session. Read it once before the first launch. L4 macOS: the per-user temp folder is writable, and it is also your own TMPDIR. A file planted there can be used by a later plain run. A session can also read /private/tmp (except Kerberos caches) and the per-user temp folder, where your own tools leave files (R's RtmpXXXX, Python temp files, other Claude Code sessions' scratch). Do not run tools that load code from TMPDIR; keep protected data out of temp folders. L5 macOS: a process that leaves the tool's process tree (a new session, a double fork) keeps running after the tool exits; launch never ends a process. Its session folder is moved to trash/ and thrown away, and a later session's folder is new, so nothing it writes there reaches a later session. It can still write the project (after the report, not reported), the spool and the per-user temp folder, and can make a folder again at its old run path (never read). Close the terminal after a session; a separate macOS user for the agent (not part of this release). L6 Carry-over (stateless): each session runs in a config folder built from a trusted copy that no session can read or write, and thrown away after it. Nothing in the tool folder is shared between sessions: no transcripts, no login, no caches, no history. On macOS two things outside it still are: the Keychain (Claude Code keeps its login there, so a session may add or change login items, including the one your plain claude uses) and the per-user temp folder, which your own tools also use. Instruction files a session changes, and the MCP and permission keys of .claude.json, go to quarantine; only what you accept (phiward carryover accept) or add yourself (phiward carryover add PATH) is trusted. A session cannot read another session's folder. Everything phiward keeps for this may be deleted at any time; you lose only what it costs to rebuild (launch.md). Login: a fresh folder means a new login each time, unless you set CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN (from claude setup-token) or ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, which the agent can read. Project memory (CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, .claude/rules/ in the project) is reported, not put back. Read the quarantine and the project report before you accept or run anything. L7 Names that a gateway command makes while it runs are not in that run's inventory, so they are not masked in its own output. The next call sees them. Print aggregates, not names (rule 3 of the agent rules in a project's AGENTS.md). L9 claude --bare and an Agent SDK app with settingSources: [] load none of phiward's wiring (hook, sandbox block, deny rules), and nothing says so. Do not use --bare on protected work; load the user settings in an SDK app or pass phiward install claude --json as its settings, or run it under phiward launch (unattended.md). L10 Linux: a folder of thousands of entries above a protected folder makes launch show that folder whole, with its protected entries masked (the view must fit in bwrap's 9000 arguments). There, a protected entry made or replaced after the start is not hidden. launch says how many folders it shows whole, and refuses when the folder that holds a protected root would have to be shown whole (it would list the root's name). Protect large data folders as roots, not one entry each among many; keep new protected data in folders that exist before the session. L8 Two sessions in one project share its write places: one can plant files that the other runs. Not confirmed in a test. Several sessions may run side by side; prefer one per project when one of them reads untrusted input.

docs.title: Agents with nobody watching: headless, the Agent SDK, scheduled runs, CI
docs.text:
• For: you, the operator, when an agent runs with no person at each step.
  • Before: the quick start is done.
  • You will have: guarded unattended runs, and a list of what holds and what does not.

An agentic workflow is a script that calls claude -p, an app built on the Claude Agent SDK, a scheduled or long-running agent, or several agents working together. phiward fits these well where it runs on your own machine, because nothing in it asks at run time. The grants are set ahead of time in your user config, and what they do not allow is refused. The limits of each mode are in modes.md and threat-model.md.

docs.title: Before every unattended run
docs.text:
phiward doctor --headless

It exits with 0 when a Claude Code session in this folder would be guarded, and with 1 and the reasons when not. Put it first in the script. A NOTE line (for example, that no rule masks subject identifiers) does not change the exit status. It checks that:

  • your user (or managed) settings run phiward's isolated hook on every tool. That is the /bin/sh -c '...; exec <python> -I -m phiward hook claude' that phiward install claude --user --write writes. The plugin's and project hooks alone are not enough here, because a project's env.PATH can replace them;
  • the program the hook names is there, every entry blocks on failure and has no async or if, and every tool is covered (the matcher *);
  • no settings file Claude Code may read turns hooks off (disableAllHooks, managed allowManagedHooksOnly) and the project's settings set no env that changes the hook;
  • the permission deny rules for protected and hidden paths are there;
  • Claude Code's sandbox confines the shell (on Linux, bubblewrap and socat are installed);
  • the broker is running.

With protected patterns, the shell counts as confined only on macOS (Claude Code 2.1.236 or newer, after install claude --user --write). Otherwise --headless reports it as not ready, because the hook then refuses shell commands other than gateway calls.

docs.title: What fits
docs.text: Workflow Set it up like this What holds claude -p in a script, cron job or LaunchAgent, on your machine (cd ~ && phiward install claude --user --write) and the broker service, as for interactive use. Never --bare. The same as an interactive session (Mode A). A refusal holds in every permission mode, bypassPermissions and dontAsk included. An Agent SDK app (Python, TypeScript) on your machine Leave settingSources at its default, or pass settings from phiward install claude --json (below). Add the callback below as a second check. Mode A, as above. The agent reads untrusted input (web pages, other people's files) Run it under Mode B: phiward launch --tool claude --report ~/phiward-runs/run.json -- claude -p "...". Read the report. The whole tool in phiward's kernel profile. Subagents, an orchestrator with workers Nothing extra. Hooks, the sandbox and deny rules apply to a subagent's tool calls too. As for the session that started them. A scheduled agent that uses HPC The shared SSH connection must be open, and your Kerberos ticket valid, when it runs. run --remote is refused (fails closed) when they have expired.

docs.title: What does not fit
docs.text:
• claude --bare, or an SDK app with settingSources: [] and nothing in its place. They load none of phiward's wiring: no hook, no sandbox block, no deny rules. Nothing says so. Claude Code's docs recommend --bare for scripts; do not use it for work beside protected data.
  • CI runners and containers that hold the data. The broker must run outside the agent, as you; in CI every other step runs as the same user, can read the data and can change your config. A broker inside a container usually cannot start its confinement, and refuses.
  • A repository you have not read. claude -p shows no trust prompt: a cloned repository's project settings (hooks, env, permission rules) apply at once. Run phiward doctor --headless in that folder first; the hook refuses every call when the project's env would change it, and the checks above name the rest.
  • GitHub-hosted runners, cloud sessions, SLURM jobs. There is no operator side there. Keep protected data away from them. Only the identifier check works without data: phiward sanitize --check FILE.

docs.title: An Agent SDK app
docs.text:
Two layers, use both.

1. The wiring as settings. An app that loads no settings file still gets phiward's hook, sandbox block and deny rules from one JSON file:

phiward install claude --json > ~/.config/phiward/sdk-settings.json

Run it in your own terminal (it prints every protected path, so it refuses without one). Put the file next to your user config: that folder is protected from agent writes (with PHIWARD_CONFIG somewhere else, beside that file). Pass it as the settings option (Python ClaudeAgentOptions(settings=...), TypeScript options.settings). Write it again after you change your phiward config.

2. A PreToolUse callback. It runs phiward's own hook on each tool call, so the decision is the same as in a Claude Code session. It judges the shell as not sandboxed (the hook is strictest then), because it cannot know which settings your app loaded. It refuses everything when phiward is missing. Copy it into your app; do not install phiward into the app's own environment (the agent may be able to change files there).

import asyncio
import json
import shutil

# your `uv tool install`, outside this app; give its full path if the app's PATH holds folders
# the agent can write (a project's .venv/bin)
PHIWARD = shutil.which("phiward")


def _deny(why):
    return {"hookSpecificOutput": {"hookEventName": "PreToolUse",
                                   "permissionDecision": "deny",
                                   "permissionDecisionReason": why}}


async def phiward_guard(input_data, tool_use_id, context):
    """PreToolUse callback: phiward's hook decides. Every failure refuses the call."""
    if PHIWARD is None:
        return _deny("phiward is not installed, so every tool call is refused")
    proc = None
    try:
        payload = dict(input_data)
        payload.pop("permission_mode", None)  # judge the shell as not sandboxed
        proc = await asyncio.create_subprocess_exec(
            PHIWARD, "hook", "claude", stdin=asyncio.subprocess.PIPE,
            stdout=asyncio.subprocess.PIPE, stderr=asyncio.subprocess.PIPE)
        out, err = await asyncio.wait_for(proc.communicate(json.dumps(payload).encode()), 30)
        if proc.returncode != 0:
            return _deny(err.decode("utf-8", "replace").strip() or "phiward refused the call")
        reply = json.loads(out) if out.strip() else {}
        decision = reply.get("hookSpecificOutput", {}).get("permissionDecision")
        if decision == "ask":
            return _deny(reply["hookSpecificOutput"].get("permissionDecisionReason",
                                                         "phiward would ask") + " (nobody to ask)")
        return reply if decision in (None, "deny") else _deny("phiward's reply was not understood")
    except Exception as exc:  # noqa: BLE001 - every failure refuses the call
        if proc is not None and proc.returncode is None:
            proc.kill()
        return _deny(f"phiward's hook did not answer ({type(exc).__name__})")

Register it for every tool:

from claude_agent_sdk import ClaudeAgentOptions, HookMatcher

options = ClaudeAgentOptions(
    settings="/Users/me/.config/phiward/sdk-settings.json",
    hooks={"PreToolUse": [HookMatcher(matcher=".*", hooks=[phiward_guard], on_failure="block")]},
)

In TypeScript, the same callback:

import { spawn, execFileSync } from "node:child_process";

// phiward from your `uv tool install`, found once, outside this app
let PHIWARD = null;
try { PHIWARD = execFileSync("sh", ["-c", "command -v phiward"]).toString().trim() || null; } catch { PHIWARD = null; }

const deny = (why) => ({ hookSpecificOutput: { hookEventName: "PreToolUse",
  permissionDecision: "deny", permissionDecisionReason: why } });

export async function phiwardGuard(input) {
  if (!PHIWARD) return deny("phiward is not installed, so every tool call is refused");
  const payload = { ...input };
  delete payload.permission_mode; // judge the shell as not sandboxed
  return await new Promise((resolve) => {
    let out = "", err = "";
    const p = spawn(PHIWARD, ["hook", "claude"], { stdio: ["pipe", "pipe", "pipe"] });
    p.stdin.on("error", () => {}); // the hook may exit before it reads; its exit decides
    const timer = setTimeout(() => { p.kill(); resolve(deny("phiward's hook did not answer")); }, 30000);
    p.on("error", () => { clearTimeout(timer); resolve(deny("phiward is not installed, so every tool call is refused")); });
    p.stdout.on("data", (d) => { out += d; });
    p.stderr.on("data", (d) => { err += d; });
    p.on("close", (code) => {
      clearTimeout(timer);
      if (code !== 0) return resolve(deny(err.trim() || "phiward refused the call"));
      let reply = {};
      try { reply = out.trim() ? JSON.parse(out) : {}; } catch { return resolve(deny("phiward's reply could not be read")); }
      const decision = reply.hookSpecificOutput?.permissionDecision;
      if (decision === "ask") {
        return resolve(deny((reply.hookSpecificOutput.permissionDecisionReason || "phiward would ask") + " (nobody to ask)"));
      }
      resolve(decision === undefined || decision === "deny" ? reply : deny("phiward's reply was not understood"));
    });
    p.stdin.end(JSON.stringify(payload));
  });
}

Register it with hooks: { PreToolUse: [{ matcher: ".*", hooks: [phiwardGuard], onFailure: "block" }] }.

The app's own code, and the tools you write into it, run as you and are not guarded by phiward: keep protected data out of them, or reach it through the gateway (phiward run).

docs.title: Mode B with nobody watching
docs.text:
phiward launch --tool claude --report ~/phiward-runs/run.json -- claude -p "count the reads per sample"

launch passes the arguments after -- to the tool and needs no terminal. Give the tool its login in CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN or ANTHROPIC_API_KEY (the agent can read it).

--report writes a JSON file whenever launch ends, also when nothing could run. A report that says needs_review: true is written before the tool starts, so a crash or a signal leaves one too. Give a file path outside every place the session can write (the project, the spool, the temp folder, ~/.phiward, in any spelling). It must not be a file that controls the guards (phiward's config or code, Claude Code's settings, a hidden credential). Otherwise nothing runs. The file is written new and moved into place, so nothing the session left at that path is opened. When the place is refused, nothing is written. For launch inside launch it is written with exit: null before the tool takes over the process (the outer launch reports the run). It holds:

  • exit: the tool's exit status;
  • ran: whether the tool started;
  • needs_review: true when the tool did not run, or the session changed instructions (they wait in quarantine), files that run later (build files, git hooks, CI workflows), settings, or git control files, or the project had more entries than launch compares. Other changed files are counted, not flagged;
  • project_changed: the changed project files by kind (instructions, runs_later, settings, other);
  • carryover: the lines about the session's instructions and quarantine;
  • git_control_changed: the git control files that changed (Linux);
  • notes: every line launch printed at the end.

A script should stop, and a person should read the notes, when needs_review is true. Accept nothing from quarantine without reading it (phiward carryover show).

docs.title: Risks that grow when nobody watches
docs.text:
• Rules that match nothing. A scheduled run whose identifier rules match none of its data looks like clean data. After it, read the broker log: no placeholder shown on a run over named data means a pack or a pattern is missing.
  • Prompt injection. A page or file the agent reads can tell it what to do, and nobody sees it happen. phiward still keeps it from reading protected data, but what it can read it can send: the network is open by default. In Mode A, [network] limit keeps shell commands to the hosts you list (configuration.md). The WebFetch tool, MCP servers and Mode B stay open.
  • Masked output is still content. Gateway output hides names and identifiers, not other content. Write the gateway commands an agent may run so that they print counts and summaries, and limit them with [broker] commands.
  • Long runs add up. Each gateway call returns up to [broker] max_output_lines lines; many calls return many lines. Set a lower limit for unattended runs, and cap the run itself (claude -p --max-turns N, the SDK's max_budget_usd).
  • Several agents share one broker and one spool. Requests carry no agent identity, and an agent can change another agent's reply in the spool (it is the same user). One agent's masked output passed to another is ordinary text to phiward.
  • Secrets in the environment. Mode A hides credential files, not environment variables. Do not put tokens an agent should not have into the environment of the run.

docs.title: Why phiward: what exists, and the gap it fills
docs.text: For: anyone who decides whether phiward is needed, beside sandboxes, containers and PII tools.

docs.title: The problem
docs.text:
An AI coding agent sends what its tools print to a model provider: file contents, command output, file names. In research on patient data, that output can hold protected health information (PHI), sample identifiers or file names that are identifiers themselves. Often there is no agreement with the provider that allows this.

People who work beside such data still want the agent's help: to write and run analyses, to check results, to submit jobs to an HPC cluster. So the question is not only "how do I keep the agent away from the data?", but also "how does the agent still work on the data, without seeing it?".

docs.title: What exists
docs.text:
This list is from each project's own documentation, read in November 2026. Check them again before you choose; they change fast.

Kind Examples What it gives What it does not give for this problem The agent tool's own sandbox and permission rules Claude Code's sandbox, permission deny rules and managed settings Bash in a kernel sandbox; file tools refused listed paths; an organization can force settings You write every path and credential by hand, per tool. No way to work on protected data with masked results. Nothing for HPC. Sandboxes around a whole command Anthropic's sandbox-runtime, nono, landrun A kernel profile (Seatbelt, bubblewrap, Landlock) around any program; network proxies A general sandbox: no model of protected data inside a readable project, no masked way back to the data, nothing for HPC. Containers and VMs Docker Sandboxes, dev containers, Apptainer Strong isolation; a session that is thrown away The data must stay outside. Docker does not run on most HPC systems. Work on the data itself is not possible from inside. Code-only PHI guards phi-guard A container that holds only the committed code; an egress firewall; masking by a cloud service Made for work away from PHI, by design. No masked way to run analyses on it. Nothing for HPC or mounted data. PII detection and redaction Presidio, LLM Guard, MCP PII proxies Finds and masks personal data in text, often with language models Sees only the text it is given. The agent's shell and file tools go around an MCP proxy. Nothing stops the agent from reading the data first. Secret scanners gitleaks and similar Find credentials in commits Not about tool output or PHI.

docs.title: The gap phiward fills
docs.text:
phiward is for work beside protected data: the agent helps with the analysis, and the data does not reach the model provider.

  1. Protected data by folder, for the whole tool. You name the folders that hold protected data once. phiward writes that into Claude Code's sandbox and permission rules (Mode A), or runs the whole tool in its own kernel profile (Mode B), together with a list of credential files that no agent may read.
  2. A masked way to work on the data. The agent does not read protected data; it asks the gateway (phiward run, phiward copy). Your broker runs the command outside the agent, as you, and masks the output: protected paths, the names of files under them, and identifier patterns become placeholders. Ask for counts and summaries: masking hides names and identifiers, not other content.
  3. HPC without giving the agent your login. phiward run --remote and phiward copy go through your own shared SSH connection. No request reads your key or Kerberos ticket, and only the hosts and programs you list are allowed.
  4. Easy for a team. One setup command, a guided setup inside Claude Code (/phiward:setup), phiward init for a project, and a check (phiward doctor) that says what is missing.
  5. Local and deterministic. No cloud service, no language model in the masking, no network. Python's standard library only.

docs.title: What phiward reuses, and what it does not do
docs.text:
• It reuses the operating system's sandboxes (Seatbelt on macOS; bubblewrap, seccomp and Landlock on Linux), Claude Code's own sandbox and permission rules, and the system ssh, tar and rsync.
  • It filters the network only where Claude Code's own sandbox can: with [network] limit, the shell commands of a Mode A session reach only the hosts you list. The WebFetch tool, MCP servers and Mode B stay open: an agent can still send what it can read there. A network proxy such as the one in sandbox-runtime could add that later.
  • Masking hides names and identifiers, not other content in a record. Gateway commands should print counts and summaries.

All limits are in threat-model.md.

docs.title: phiward v0.2.0b1 (beta)
docs.text:
The first public release of phiward. It keeps protected data (for example patient data) and your credentials out of what an AI coding agent sends to its model provider.

Start with docs/quickstart.md: install phiward, set it up (with Claude Code's help through /phiward:setup, or by hand), and check it.

uv tool install --python-preference only-managed phiward==0.2.0b1

Or from the GitHub tag: uv tool install git+https://github.com/msk-access/phiward@v0.2.0b1.

docs.title: What you get
docs.text:
• Mode A, the default: every normal Claude Code session (the desktop app, an IDE, a terminal) is wired by phiward install claude --user. Bash runs in Claude Code's sandbox, the file tools are refused protected data and credentials, and every session starts with a note on the rules.
  • Mode B, the stronger one: phiward launch --tool claude runs the whole tool (file tools, shell, MCP servers, hooks) in phiward's kernel profile. Terminal only for now.
  • The gateway: the agent works on protected data only through phiward run and phiward copy. The broker runs them outside the agent and masks the output.
  • HPC through your own shared SSH connection: phiward run --remote and phiward copy. No request reads your key or Kerberos ticket (hpc.md).
  • Easy onboarding: a Claude Code plugin with /phiward:setup, /phiward:doctor and /phiward:help; phiward init for a project; phiward mcp, the gateway as MCP tools (plugins.md).
  • The broker as a login service: phiward broker --service --write.

A summary of this release is in the CHANGELOG.

docs.title: Tested, on made-up data
docs.text:
• Mode A in the Claude Code desktop app on macOS: reads of protected data and of a credential by the Read tool, cat and Monitor were refused; ssh to HPC failed; normal work was unaffected.
  • The plugin in a desktop-app session: the session note, the refusals, the commands, normal work; and beside another plugin (ECC).
  • Mode B with the real Claude Code on macOS: the file tools and the shell were refused protected data; the gateway returned masked output; a skill and an MCP server carried over.
  • HPC against a real cluster: remote runs, a push, a pull into a protected folder, and the refusals.
  • An MCP server wrapped in phiward launch, on macOS and Linux.
  • The full test suite on macOS and Linux; fuzz tests; several adversarial reviews.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
All limits are in docs/threat-model.md, with a summary for reviewers at the top. The main ones:

  • Identifiers inside files need a pack or patterns. Out of the box, masking inside file contents covers only sequence and alignment file names, read names and loci (the genomics pack). Subject and sample identifiers inside files are masked only with a pack that has them (the msk example), your own [sanitize] patterns or names_from. The gateway masks entry names under the protected roots (4 characters or longer). Planned for 0.2.0b2: setup asks, doctor warns, and the output says what was masked (#3, #5).
  • The network is open by default. [network] limit (asked by setup) limits the shell commands of a Mode A session to listed hosts; WebFetch, MCP servers and Mode B stay open. The agent cannot read protected data, but it can send what it can read.
  • Masking covers names and identifiers, not content. Print counts and summaries through the gateway.
  • In Mode A, the file tools are refused inside Claude Code, not by the kernel, and hooks and MCP servers that are not wrapped run with your rights.
  • run --remote is not confined on the cluster. [remote] commands is what limits it.
  • macOS: the Keychain and the per-user temp folder are shared with your own tools.
